title: V Stock Slips After-Hours — Visa Reports $563M Job Cut-Related Costs Amid Resilient Consumer Spending - Stocktwits
content: Visa Inc. (V) reported higher fiscal third-quarter revenue and adjusted profits, powered by resilient consumer spending and continued expansion in international transaction volumes. The San Francisco-based payments engine recorded quarterly net revenue of $11.63 billion for the period ended June 30, marking a 14% increase from $10.17 billion in the same quarter a year earlier and above analyst expectations of $11.4 billion, as per Fiscal.ai. Earnings for the quarter amounted to $3.32 per share up 11% from a year prior and above expectations of $3.23 per share. "Visa delivered a strong fiscal third quarter... Consumer and business spending remains resilient, and our strategy continues to deliver strong performance across consumer payments, commercial and money movement solutions and value-added services," said Chief Executive Officer Ryan McInerney. Operational metrics remained healthy across all core divisions. Global payments volume grew 10% year-over-year on a constant-dollar basis, while total cross-border volume expanded 13%. Excluding intra-Europe transactions, cross-border volume surged 12%. Data processing revenue jumped 17% to $6.04 billion, service revenue rose 14% to $4.92 billion, and international transaction revenue climbed 6% to $3.85 billion. Total operating expenses grew 19% on a GAAP basis to $4.76 billion, driven largely by higher personnel costs and legal reserves, alongside an 18% increase in client incentive outlays to $4.68 billion. The quarter’s results were tempered by significant restructuring charges. Visa recorded a $563 million pre-tax special item in severance costs. The workforce reductions reflect ongoing efforts by the card processor to streamline operational efficiencies and reallocate resources toward high-growth technological initiatives, including tokenization and automated money movement solutions. In addition to severance expenses, results were impacted by a $237-million litigation provision related to long-standing legal disputes. Shares of Replimune Group Inc (REPL) closed 38% lower on Tuesday, clocking its worst day since early April, after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration released documents that put a possible approval for its experimental cancer drug in question. Wall Street now views the path to clearance for RP1 as increasingly uncertain following two prior rejections. Replimune is seeking accelerated approval for RP1 in combination with nivolumab for certain advanced melanoma patients who progressed after anti-PD-1 therapy. This is the company’s third attempt. The FDA issued complete response letters in July 2025 and April 2026. Both letters said the single-arm mid-stage IGNYTE trial was not an adequate and well-controlled study. Regulators flagged two main problems: the trial could not clearly show how much of the benefit came from RP1 versus nivolumab alone, and the mixed patient group made the results hard to interpret. In June, the agency accepted Replimune’s latest resubmission, set an August 2 decision deadline, and scheduled an advisory committee meeting for July 30. The FDA documents released earlier on Tuesday, ahead of the committee meeting, repeated the core objection: the application still lacks an adequate, well-controlled investigation that demonstrates substantial evidence of effectiveness. Wedbush said the FDA is sticking to its guns, noting inadequacies in the IGNYTE study design and unclear contribution of components. The firm nonetheless anticipates a favorable panel vote on whether the efficacy results are evaluable and clinically meaningful, citing a clear response advantage over historical outcomes with immune-checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy alone. Panelists are expected to find the signal persuasive, though Wedbush remains guarded on final approval odds given the agency’s strongly critical stance. Wedbush carries a Neutral rating on REPL and a $9 price target, implying a potential upside of 4% from Tuesday’s close. BMO Capital’s Evan Seigerman, meanwhile, described the briefing documents as negative in tone. BMO sees Replimune facing a difficult session at Thursday’s meeting, with the agency appearing consistent with the positions taken in earlier complete response letters. The firm rates the shares Outperform with a $16 target, suggesting 85% upside. But a day before the earnings, Deepwater Asset Management’s Gene Munster said investors should look beyond the results, adding that the software giant faces longer-term challenges from artificial intelligence and changes to its business model. MSFT shares ended the regular session up about 1% and had added another 0.25% in after-hours trading at the time of writing. Ahead of the earnings report, Munster said in a post on X that Microsoft’s earnings “don’t matter” because its “battle with the bots is just beginning.” He said the company faces two major headwinds over the next five years that could make the stock a “value trap,” even if the shares rise following the results. Munster said, “They need to restructure their business model from per-seat to usage-based.” While he expects Azure to “crush it” over the next few years, he adds that the company’s “core business needs a new pricing model.” He said Microsoft hinted at the shift last quarter and investors are likely to hear more with the upcoming earnings report. However, Munster warned that “new business model = uncertainty = low multiple,” suggesting the transition could weigh on the company’s valuation. Munster said Microsoft’s “battle with the bots” is just beginning, adding that even if the company reports impressive earnings, the “bot boogeyman will not go away.” He added, “The reason is the utility of software is based on the abstraction layer (the ability of humans to interface with the machine). Agents and bots remove the need for the abstraction layer because they just need bot-talk.” While acknowledging how entrenched Microsoft’s products are, citing his daily use of Excel as an example, Munster said “entrenchment” is a relative term when AI has the potential to rebuild business processes from the ground up. Shares of health insurance companies, including Centene (CNC), slipped after-hours on Tuesday following a report that the Trump administration plans to end a federal subsidy program that has helped suppress Medicare Part D prescription drug plan premiums. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. CNC shares dived 3% after hours on Tuesday, while shares of UNH, CVS, and HUM fell by about or less than 1%. Bloom Energy (BE) share price soared 10% after-hours on Tuesday after the company raised its 2026 full-year revenue outlook and beat earnings and revenue expectations for the second quarter owing to rising energy demand from hyperscalers and AI labs. The fuel-cell-based energy provider reported earnings of $0.78 per share on revenue of $1.07 billion for the second quarter. Wall Street is expecting the company to post 106% revenue growth to $827.02 million in Q2, while earnings per share are expected to grow more than 4x to $0.41, as per data from Fiscal.ai. During Tuesday’s regular session, BE stock ended about 11.3% lower as investors contemplated the range of revenue growth following recent short seller reports claiming the company’s supply chain was overreliant on China, which sent the stock tumbling. However, the company, in an emailed statement as well as through an 8-K filing, mentioned that it does not rely on China for its scandium needs. “Customers are now placing longer-term orders leading to our backlog growing at a faster pace than revenue,” KR Sridhar, CEO of Bloom Energy, said during the earnings call. Bloom updated its full-year 2026 revenue forecast to $3.9 - $4.2 billion from $3.4 - $3.8 billion forecast in the previous quarter. The updated figure now places its revenue at double that of its full-year 2025 revenue. The updated forecasts come in the wake of a surge in demand for onsite power solutions as hyperscalers increasingly choose fuel cells over combustion-based technologies. The firm also updated its 2026 earnings projections to $2.55 - $2.85 per share from $1.85 - $2.25 per share projected at the end of the first quarter. title: "It's already started.." BTS V and Cho Seong-jin film each other performing.. Heartwarming and moving - starnewskorea.com
content:
BTS member V shared a video of pianist Cho Seong-jin playing the piano on his Instagram story, drawing attention from fans around the world. In the video, V performed the jazz standard "Misty," composed by pianist Erroll Garner in 1954. Through the glass window, it was also visible that V was filming Cho Seong-jin's performance of Chopin's Ballade No. 4. Cho Seong-jin mentioned in a MasterClass interview after releasing his first studio album in November 2016 regarding the scene where he slowly parts the air with his left hand before playing the piano keys, saying, "We don't start this, it's already started." This means that the music has already begun even before the first note is played, and the airflow and tension before the performer intentionally produces sound are also part of the music. V quoted the phrase "It's already started.." from Cho Seong-jin, slowly placing his fingers on the piano keys while performing "Misty." Cho Seong-jin directly referenced the phrase he himself had said, "It's already started," while playing Chopin's Ballade No. 4. V, who has stated that he is practicing the piano, said in his closing remarks at the Goyang concert of the April "Arirang Tour" that he was looking for a piano teacher. During a live broadcast in 2019, he revealed that he is a fan of Cho Seong-jin, saying, "I often watch Cho Seong-jin's videos. If I get the chance, I want to attend his concerts." V watched Cho Seong-jin's Lisa concert with director Park Chan-wook in June and, in July, shared a three-shot photo taken outdoors with Son Heung-min and Cho Seong-jin along with a birthday message for Son Heung-min. title: “Related” But Not Excluded: Delaware Court Rejects Insurer’s Narrow View of D&O Coverage for Derivative Claim - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. Policyholders facing “related” claim denials under D&O policies should take note of the recent Delaware Superior Court decision, Big V Capital LLC v. Great American Insurance Company (Del. Super. June 30, 2026), where the court held that a derivative action filed during a renewal policy period was covered—even though it was related to an earlier books-and-records action that the policyholder had not reported under the prior policy. The decision turned on the specific structure and wording of the policy at issue but reinforces core policyholder-friendly principles under Delaware law, including construing coverage broadly while refusing to deny claims absent a clear and specific exclusion. A minority member of a commercial real estate firm brought a books-and-records action, alleging suspected misuse of company assets by the firm’s member-manager. The company did not seek coverage or provide notice of the action to its D&O insurer, and the action later settled after the company produced records. A few months later, after the company’s D&O policy had renewed, the same minority member filed a direct and derivative action against the company, related entities, and the member-manager. The complaint alleged fiduciary-duty breaches arising from the alleged diversion of company assets. The company noticed and sought coverage for the derivative action under the renewal policy. The insurer denied the claim, contending that the derivative action was “interrelated” with the earlier books-and-records action and thus was deemed a single claim first made at the time of the original claim, outside the covered renewal policy period. The insurer also concluded that it was too late for the insureds to seek coverage under the earlier policy period. The insureds sued the insurer in Delaware state court, seeking a declaration that coverage exists for the derivative action and damages for breach of the policy. After the parties filed competing dispositive motions, the key question was whether the renewal policy barred coverage for related matters that would otherwise be available under the insuring agreement covering claims first made during the renewal period. The parties did not dispute that the books-and-records action and the derivative action were meaningfully linked and, therefore, involved related claims. But that was not enough to defeat coverage. As the court explained, whether related claims are deemed first made at the time of an earlier matter “for coverage purposes” depends on the policy language. The insurer relied principally on a related-claim provision in the policy’s retention section. That provision stated that claims involving the same or interrelated wrongful acts would constitute a single claim and would be deemed made on the earliest date of either a related claim or notice of related wrongful acts. The insurer characterized this provision as a “deemer” clause that defined the “relevant timeline” for when claims are deemed made as a general matter. The court disagreed and found the insurer’s interpretation to be unreasonable. The related-claim provision appeared in the policy’s retentions section and was expressly geared at relatedness in the context of retentions, allowing the policyholder to pay just one retention for several claims alleging interrelated wrongful acts. It did not exclude coverage for a claim first made during the policy period merely because it related to an earlier, unreported matter. The policy also contained a “related claims” exclusion. That exclusion barred coverage for claims involving wrongful acts or interrelated wrongful acts but only when those acts had been the subject of an earlier notice or claim under a prior policy. Because the earlier books-and-records action had not been reported, the exclusion did not apply. Accepting the insurer’s broad reading of the retention provision, the court explained, would render the related-claims exclusion meaningless by barring coverage for all prior related matters, reported or unreported. The insurer therefore had not shown that the otherwise-covered derivative action was specifically excluded. This decision provides several useful lessons for policyholders: Related-claims disputes are inherently fact, policy, and jurisdiction-specific. Aside from the variations in common law standards for “interrelatedness,” material differences in policy language and structure can shift related claims in or out of coverage depending on the specific facts of the claim. Here, because the earlier books-and-records action was not reported, the prior-notice-based related-claims exclusion did not apply, leaving coverage available for the later derivative action. title: The Japanese Hybrid SUV That’s Worth Every Penny - Top Speed
content: Hybrid SUVs have firmly moved from niche curiosity to mainstream must-have in the U.S. market — and it's easy to see why. By pairing efficient internal combustion engines with compact electric motors, they deliver real-world fuel savings without the range anxiety or charging-infrastructure headaches that come with a fully electric vehicle. They also tend to carry friendlier price tags than their battery-only counterparts, making the transition to electrified motoring far more accessible for everyday buyers. That growing demand has pushed virtually every major automaker to field a gasoline-electric version of its best-selling crossover, turning the segment into one of the most competitive — and consumer-friendly — corners of the new-car market. The result is a wide field of capable, well-equipped options, each brand striving to out-value the next. Sitting at the top of that field is a popular Japanese model from a brand with a long, proven track record in hybrid engineering.     Based on its popularity, we can comfortably say that it is well worth the competitive asking price. It's a nameplate that has been on U.S. roads for several decades, and one that has benefited from a hybrid drivetrain offered in both front-wheel drive and all-wheel drive configurations. It has become so successful for its Japanese manufacturer that it effectively outshines every other vehicle in the brand's current lineup. This article has been updated to include more information regarding long-term ownership costs. Many     would think that the Toyota RAV4 Hybrid is the best hybrid crossover option that you can consider, but the Honda CR-V Hybrid presents itself as a more comprehensive package. A big reason for its market success is the impressive gasoline-electric powertrain, which pairs a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with two permanent-magnet motors. Honda offers the CR-V Hybrid with a choice of front- or all-wheel drivetrains, both of which produce a combined 204 horsepower and 247 pound-feet of torque delivered through a direct-drive eCVT. Honda claims an 8.0-second 0–60 mph time for the front-wheel drive model and a 7.6-second time for the all-wheel drive variant. Independent tests suggest these figures hold up well in real-world conditions. Honda limits both drivetrains to a 111 mph top speed. Unlike the RAV4, Honda routes drive to the rear wheels through a conventional driveline rather than a dedicated rear electric motor — which is why the combined output figure stays the same regardless of which drivetrain you choose. The Honda CR-V's hybrid system employs a supplementary 1.1 kWh lithium-ion battery pack, resulting in a strong 40/34/37 MPG EPA estimate on the city/highway/combined cycle for the front-wheel drive option. The all-wheel drive model returns a slightly lower 37/34/37 MPG result. The 14-gallon fuel tank provides up to 560 miles of range in front-wheel drive form, dropping to 518 miles with all-wheel drive. Honda's hybrid system is a series-parallel design, meaning the electric motor can operate independently of the combustion engine. The eCVT uses a clutch-based arrangement that also allows the motor to function as a generator for auxiliary loads, including the starter and climate control. Again, unlike Toyota, Honda applies this same drivetrain architecture to other models in its lineup, namely the     Civic and Accord Hybrid. The Accord benefits from higher power outputs, while the Civic is marginally less powerful. It's also worth noting that the Accord's front-wheel drive and all-wheel drive variants produce different combined output figures. The CR-V Hybrid outsells its sedan stablemates because it offers greater versatility, capability, and practicality — qualities that are increasingly valued as crossovers continue to displace traditional sedans and coupes across the industry. The Honda CR-V has long enjoyed a strong reliability reputation, and the current generation is no exception. Consumer Reports gives the model a predicted reliability rating of 54/100 — admittedly modest — but its 4/5 owner satisfaction score and 93/100 road test rating inspire considerable confidence, lifting its overall score to an impressive 84/100. J.D. Power awards the entire CR-V range an 84/100 quality and reliability rating, placing it among the most dependable models in its segment. That said, the CR-V Hybrid has been subject to recalls relating to a leaking fuel pump and a faulty steering gear spring, both of which Honda rectifies at no cost to the owner. According to iSeeCars, the CR-V has an average lifespan of around 169,626 miles or about 13.9 years, with a 30.4 percent chance of reaching 200,000 miles. The publication grants it a 7.9/10 for reliability, placing it in second place for both most reliable crossover SUV and most reliable small SUV categories. CarEdge placed the CR-V's five-year cost at $36,935, which is just over $1,000 more than the RAV4. In terms of maintenance costs, CarEdge puts the dollar amount at $7,636 over the first ten years of ownership, with a 21.74 percent chance it will require major repairs - both of those figures are lower than the average for similar SUVs. Honda includes its standard three-year or 36,000-mile limited warranty and five-year or 60,000-mile powertrain warranty with every CR-V Hybrid. You also receive a five-year corrosion warranty with no mileage cap. Replacement parts fitted by the dealer are covered for one year, and accessories carry a three-year or 46,000-mile warranty. The hybrid system itself is covered for three years or 36,000 miles, while the battery pack receives the industry-standard eight years and 100,000 miles of coverage. For added peace of mind on the road, every CR-V Hybrid also includes a 36-month or 36,000-mile roadside assistance plan. Honda also offers in-house extended warranty packages in various term and mileage combinations for buyers who plan to keep the vehicle long-term. The CR-V Hybrid isn't Honda's most affordable model, but it is very competitively positioned within its segment. Even at the base Sport Hybrid trim level, which starts at $35,630, the standard equipment list is genuinely comprehensive, covering most of the essentials buyers expect at this price point. All-wheel drive is available on the Sport and Sport-L trims for an additional charge, while the flagship Sport Touring comes exclusively with all-wheel drive and starts at $42,550. Prices quoted exclude Honda's destination and handling fee. Options and packages are focused on all-season equipment and cosmetic upgrades for buyers who want a more distinctive look, along with a selection of optional exterior colors. All trims come standard with front heated seats, dual-zone climate control, a six-speaker audio system, and Honda's touchscreen infotainment system. The Sport-L adds a wireless smartphone charger, leather upholstery, more premium exterior trim, an eight-speaker audio system, and a larger 9.0-inch touchscreen. The Sport Touring brings a Bose premium audio system, power-adjustable front seats with memory functions, and a heated steering wheel — and is available exclusively with all-wheel drive. Honda offers several optional packages across all trims, including all-weather accessories and the HPD performance-inspired visual kit. Be sure to factor in the brand's destination fee when budgeting. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: Double Books and Disguised Payees: Corporate Personal Expenses and the Civil Fraud Penalty in Prezioso v. Commissioner - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. The taxpayer, Walter D. Prezioso, joined GSP Precision, Inc. (GSP)—an aerospace manufacturing company incorporated under California law in 1983 by his father, Juan Pablo Prezioso, and George J. Gottardi—as an employee in 1992. Following Walter’s acquisition of a 25% interest in GSP from his father in 1997, George retained a 50% interest, while Juan Pablo and Walter each held 25%. In 2001, GSP’s board of directors adopted a resolution designating Walter’s signature as the sole requirement for any checks issued by GSP. By June 2002, George and Juan Pablo effectively retired from GSP’s day-to-day operations, vesting Walter with sole authority over day-to-day operations and future employment decisions, except for the employment of family members. Walter turned the company's declining financials around and became chief executive officer in 2007. The Court found that beginning in 2007, GSP began paying certain personal expenses for Walter. GSP's board minutes dated December 22, 2009, authorized GSP to "continue to pay personal leased vehicle, vehicle insurance, gas, family medical insurance, Sentry life insurance[,] and credit card expenses for lunch, dinner, customer expenses[,] or company expenses." However, the Court found that GSP paid for a vast array of Walter's personal expenses that far exceeded those authorized by the board. Specifically, the Court found that GSP paid for Walter’s "personal credit cards, home renovations, a home-equity line of credit, landscaping services, tennis court and pool contractors, and audio/visual equipment." GSP also paid Walter’s boat and recreational vehicle loans and leased vehicles on his behalf, issuing over 400 checks for Walter’s personal expenses during the tax years in issue (2009–12). The Court found that for all years in issue except 2012, "the amounts GSP paid for Walter’s personal expenses exceeded the losses reported on its Forms 1120, U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return." None of these payments were reported on Forms W-2 or Forms 1099-MISC issued to Walter, exempting them from payroll taxes and federal income tax reporting. Nonetheless, the Court found that Walter understood these benefits were compensatory, noting that on a credit application for a Ferrari lease, Walter listed his income as "Verifiable $52,950 W-2" and "Actual $275,000." Walter and his wife, Kimberly J. Prezioso, timely filed joint Forms 1040 for the 2009 through 2013 tax years, reporting Walter’s W-2 salary but omitting all income attributable to GSP's payment of their personal expenses. On December 20, 2023, the IRS issued Notices of Deficiency, determining federal income tax deficiencies and civil fraud penalties for all years in issue. Petitioners subsequently conceded the underlying deficiencies for all tax years, as well as the fraud penalty for tax year 2013, leaving only the civil fraud penalties for tax years 2009–12 for decision by the Tax Court. In their request for relief, petitioners characterized their underpayments as the result of an "honest mistake" or poor judgment, and Walter testified that he was not aware at the time that GSP's payment of his personal expenses constituted taxable income. He further testified that he believed these expenses were being correctly reported on GSP's corporate returns. Under I.R.C. § 6663(a), "if any part of any underpayment of tax required to be shown on a return is due to fraud," a penalty of 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud is imposed. The Commissioner bears the burden of proving fraud by "clear and convincing evidence" under I.R.C. § 7454(a) and Tax Court Rule 142(b). This requires establishing two distinct elements: (1) that there was an underpayment of tax for each year in issue, and (2) that at least some portion of the underpayment for each year was due to fraud. See Hebrank v. Commissioner, 81 T.C. 640, 642 (1983). When the Commissioner asserts fraud penalties for multiple tax years, this burden "applies separately for each of the years." See Vanover v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-79; Temple v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2000-337, aff'd, 62 F. App'x 605 (6th Cir. 2003). Furthermore, under I.R.C. § 7491(c), the Commissioner bears the burden of production with respect to an individual taxpayer's liability for any penalty, requiring sufficient evidence indicating that the penalty is appropriate. See Higbee v. Commissioner, 116 T.C. 438, 446–47 (2001). As part of this burden, the Commissioner must produce evidence of compliance with the written supervisory approval requirement of I.R.C. § 6751(b). See Graev v. Commissioner, 149 T.C. 485, 492–93 (2017). In this case, because petitioners conceded the deficiencies, the IRS easily carried its burden regarding underpayments. The IRS also met its burden of production under I.R.C. § 6751(b) by showing that Group Manager Anet Magadamyan approved the civil fraud penalties by executing a Civil Penalty Approval Form on July 9, 2021. Prior to analyzing the fraud penalties, the Court resolved an evidentiary issue regarding the admissibility of testimony by George Gottardi’s son, Fernando Gottardi. In 2013, Fernando sought GSP employment and was rebuffed by Walter. Following this disagreement, Fernando analyzed GSP’s financials, identified discrepancies, and prompted George and Marta to file a shareholder-derivative suit in July 2013, which ultimately placed GSP into receivership and led to its February 3, 2014, voluntary petition for bankruptcy protection. The IRS filed a Motion in Limine asking the Court to admit Fernando’s testimony, arguing that his investigation gave context to the shareholder suit and was relevant to evaluating Walter’s credibility. However, the Court excluded the testimony, explaining that the IRS failed to establish that Fernando had "firsthand knowledge of any relevant facts" during the years in issue. Citing Colvin v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-26, the Court ruled that because Fernando's testimony merely summarized and offered opinions on otherwise admissible documents, it was not relevant to the factual issues to be decided. Because direct proof of fraudulent intent is rarely available, the Court emphasized that "fraudulent intent may be established by circumstantial evidence." See Petzoldt v. Commissioner, 92 T.C. 661, 699 (1989). To sustain his burden, the Commissioner must show that "the taxpayer intended to evade taxes known to be owing by conduct intended to conceal, mislead, or otherwise prevent the collection of taxes." See Parks v. Commissioner, 94 T.C. 654, 661 (1990). The Court may examine "the taxpayer’s entire course of conduct" to infer this intent. See Webb v. Commissioner, 394 F.2d 366, 379 (5th Cir. 1968); Stone v. Commissioner, 56 T.C. 213, 224 (1971). To evaluate circumstantial intent, courts rely on the well-known "badges of fraud" set forth in Bradford v. Commissioner, 796 F.2d 303, 307–08 (9th Cir. 1986). These badges include: The Tax Court noted that while the existence of any single badge is not dispositive, "the existence of several badges is persuasive circumstantial evidence of fraud." See Niedringhaus v. Commissioner, 99 T.C. 202, 211 (1992). A central pillar of the Court's finding of fraudulent intent was Walter’s double bookkeeping system. GSP had no on-staff accountant, leaving Walter primarily responsible for entering checks and invoices into GSP's bookkeeping software. The Court found that this process resulted in two distinct sets of charts of accounts: "an internal set provided to GSP shareholders for periodic review (Internal Charts) and an external set provided to Mr. Caven for accounting and tax purposes (Accountant Charts)." In the Internal Charts, the Court found that Walter systematically disguised the payment of his personal expenses by entering different, false payee names, which were usually existing GSP business vendors. For example, the Court found that two checks dated February 2, 2011, payable to "Chase Card" for Walter’s personal credit cards, were falsely recorded in the Internal Charts as payable to Cowan Precision Grinding and Quality Heat Treating, Inc. Other entries substituted payees like Harvey Titanium, Titanium Industries, and Service Steel for the actual payee, Chase Card. The Court found that Walter changed payee names for his personal expenses even when GSP was simultaneously paying legitimate business expenses to the same vendor. In October 2007, GSP issued two checks to Washington Mutual; Walter recorded the business expense check correctly, but recorded the personal expense check in the Internal Charts as payable to "A.M. Castle & Co." Direct payments to Walter and his father were entirely omitted from the Internal Charts. In contrast, when generating the Accountant Charts at the end of each month to send to Mr. Caven, Walter’s standard practice was to change the payee names in the bookkeeping software back to the correct payee names (though he failed to do so for at least three expenses in December 2011). After exporting the Accountant Charts, Walter would change the payee names back to the incorrect ones in the software. Furthermore, the Court found that Walter manipulated GSP's expense coding. GSP's outside CPA, John Caven of Caven & Associates, had established specific expense codes, including Code 4710 for material purchases, Code 4711 for outside processing, Code 4715 for equipment rental, Code 4718 for equipment repair, and separate codes for officer compensation and shareholder draws. The Court found that Walter coded many personal expenses as equipment repair, then modified the code to material purchases or outside processing (and added a false payee name) for the Internal Charts, before reverting them to equipment repair for the Accountant Charts. Other personal expenses, such as the Chase credit card charges, were coded as material purchases and left unchanged for the Accountant Charts. Because these personal expenses were classified as material purchases, outside processing, or equipment repair, they were aggregated on GSP's profit and loss statements as "Cost of Sales" and capitalized as "cost of goods sold" on GSP’s corporate tax returns (Forms 1120). The Court rejected petitioners' argument that the Internal Charts were kept merely for the non-tax purpose of hiding Walter’s personal expenses from envious GSP employees. The Court clarified that "a taxpayer’s practice of double bookkeeping, even where the fraudulent set of books was kept for nontax purposes, is indicative of fraudulent intent." See Podlucky v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2022-45, aff'd, No. 22-70169, 2024 WL 4234510 (9th Cir. Sep. 19, 2024). The Court further held that Walter's bookkeeping practices resulted in "providing incomplete or misleading information" to Mr. Caven, another powerful badge of fraud. The Court emphasized that "a taxpayer who relies on a return preparer may not withhold information from the return preparer and then 'escape responsibility for the false tax returns which result.'" See United States v. Garavaglia, 566 F.2d 1056, 1060 (6th Cir. 1977). Under long-standing precedent, "keeping two sets of books is circumstantial evidence of fraudulent intent." See Benavides & Co., P.C. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-115; Potter v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-18; Karcho v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2000-213. Under established federal tax law, a corporation’s payment of a shareholder’s personal expenses generally constitutes taxable income to the shareholder, as either compensation or constructive dividends. See Barrington v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2022-68; see also Helvering v. Horst, 311 U.S. 112, 119 (1940). The Court found that petitioners consistently and substantially underreported their income across all tax years in issue. Although a mere understatement of income is not alone proof of fraud, "the consistent and substantial understatement of income is strong evidence of it." See Truesdell v. Commissioner, 89 T.C. 1280, 1302 (1987); Marcus v. Commissioner, 70 T.C. 562, 577 (1978). The Court dismissed Walter’s defense that the underreporting resulted from an honest mistake. It pointed to his credit application for a Ferrari lease—where he listed his verifiable income as $52,950 but his actual income as $275,000—as clear evidence that Walter understood his actual income was far greater than what was reported to the IRS. Additionally, the Court highlighted Walter’s willful blindness. Walter executed GSP's corporate returns (Forms 1120) for the 2009 through 2011 tax years. He admitted at trial that he did not thoroughly review them or inquire about their accuracy, despite his highly irregular bookkeeping practices and the corporate losses generated by his personal expenditures. The Court held that "a trier of fact may infer that an individual knew of his or her evasion of tax from his or her willful blindness to the existence of that fact." See Fields v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1996-425. The Court also rejected Walter’s attempt to shift blame onto GSP’s deceased accountant, Mr. Caven. Since Mr. Caven had created detailed expense codes for officer compensation and draws, it was highly implausible that he would instruct Walter to code personal items as "equipment repair" or "material purchases." The Court held that providing trial testimony that lacks credibility is a distinct badge of fraud. See Beleiu v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2025-70; Morse v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2003-332, aff'd, 419 F.3d 829 (8th Cir. 2005). Finally, the Court connected Walter’s willingness to deceive GSP’s other shareholders through the Internal Charts to his tax fraud, noting that "a taxpayer’s dishonesty in business transactions or willingness to defraud others may indicate a willingness to defraud the Commissioner." See Solomon v. Commissioner, 732 F.2d 1459, 1462 (6th Cir. 1984); McGee v. Commissioner, 61 T.C. 249, 260 (1973); Ferguson v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2004-90. In sum, the Tax Court found clear and convincing evidence of civil fraud under I.R.C. § 6663(a) with respect to all years in issue, citing Walter’s double bookkeeping, implausible explanations, and active efforts to conceal the payment arrangement. Although there was no finding that Kimberly J. Prezioso participated in the fraud, the Court confirmed she remained jointly and severally liable for the deficiencies and fraud penalties because they filed joint returns. Under I.R.C. § 6013(d)(3), spouses filing a joint return are each fully responsible for the accuracy of their return and are jointly and severally liable for the entire tax and penalties found to be owed. See Butler v. Commissioner, 114 T.C. 276, 282 (2000). Copyright © 2025 Thomas, Zollars & Lynch, Ltd., All Rights Reserved

title: The Cadillac CT4-V Blackwing Is A Better BMW M3 For $15,000 Less - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update When it comes to sports sedans, there's probably no better choice than the BMW M3. Since the 1980s, it's backed up its iconic status with supercar-beating performance and versatility, but the market is more competitive now than ever. Cadillac is one of its biggest rivals here in the States – and that's because the CT4-V Blackwing offers the same power for $15,000 less. So why does BMW charge so much more for its evergreen sedan? Some might say you're only paying for the badge, while others will say that nothing compares to how a BMW handles. We're taking a deep dive into these two cars to see where that extra money goes – or whether you should simply save some money and buy American. The first thing you're going to want in your sports sedan is power – and both of these cars have that in spades. The Cadillac CT4-V Blackwing, which goes for $62,700 at MSRP, comes with only one power output option, thanks to its 3.6L twin-turbo V6 engine. Its 472 horsepower and 445 pound-feet of torque are yours to harness, which is actually almost exactly the same power output as the BMW M3. That car has a 3.0L twin-turbo inline-six. The key difference, though, is the level of customization available with the BMW's performance outputs. The base model makes 473 hp, but the Competition models make either 503 or 523 hp depending on RWD or AWD configurations. These models are significantly more expensive, though, and you lose the purity of rear-wheel drive. The BMW ($78,400 MSRP) gets to 60 mph only 0.2 seconds faster (4.1 seconds as opposed to 4.3 seconds), but you'll probably never feel that difference. Both of these cars are about how they make you feel, which is why they come with six-speed manual transmissions, sport brakes, and adaptive suspension as standard. Cadillac claims its adaptive system – Magnetic Ride Control – is the fastest-reacting system in the world, and it has been known to be softer than rivals when simply cruising on the highway. For that, the Caddy also has SuperCruise hands-free driving, which helps take the strain off on a road trip. "While the Cadillac's twin-turbocharged V6 may not offer the turbine smoothness of an inline-six, it works very well alongside the standard manual transmission to get the little Caddy up to speed in between corners. It's the last true compact sports sedan, and it's a blast to drive in almost any situation." – Brett Evans, senior road tester, CarBuzz If all you want is power and driving experience, you can't go wrong with saving some money and going with the CT4-V Blackwing. The manual is engaging, the limited-slip differential means it's controllable, and when you're not traveling at speed, the suspension is more compliant than the race-ready BMW M3. We were all quite surprised when we first saw the kidney grilles on the current-generation BMW M3. Usually, an M3 would have pretty subtle styling cues compared to the regular 3-Series, but this car went fully in on the aggressiveness for cooling and design purposes. It has divided opinion, and that's why the more affordable Cadillac's styling appeals more to most people's tastes. Yes, there are occasional aero flicks and spoilers, but we think it works better as a sleeper sports sedan than the German alternative. Even the color and aesthetic choices lean toward subtlety on the Cadillac, while BMW's palette is designed to attract attention through bright colors. Both let you change the brake caliper colors, and if you want to show people you have a Blackwing, you can option some decals and carbon fiber packages. The same theme continues inside as the Cadillac retains physical controls to aid usability when on the move. It may look more dated than the BMW, but we'd rather have buttons that are easy to press while driving than a display that looks cleaner when turned off. Both can be chosen with bucket seats, although the BMW's are more expensive and feature an odd central element that can be uncomfortable to use with a manual. Like the exterior, the inside of the BMW looks racier, especially when you choose the expensive carbon fiber trim options. Cadillac looks to be leaning into the "everyday" usage of the sedan, with accessories for all-weather cargo mats, cargo nets, and even organizers. They might not be the first thing you associate with a sports car, but they're genuinely useful for a daily driver. Even when saving money by choosing the Cadillac, you aren't sacrificing many creature comforts. The Cadillac has a 15-speaker sound system, heated front seats, and wireless charging. We'd also recommend optioning the affordable climate package, which includes ventilated seats, a heated steering wheel, and even lumbar massage – a feature not available on the BMW at all. Just ventilated seating costs $500 on the BMW. "The biggest dynamic advantage of the Cadillac CT4-V Blackwing is its stiff Alpha architecture and genuinely compact size and weight. Compared to the G80 M3, the Blackwing is lighter on its feet and feels more responsive." – Brett Evans, senior road tester, CarBuzz For performance, both vehicles can be fitted with lap time optimizers and analysis, but Cadillac's system is more advanced and can record video as well as data. It's more expensive, but if you're going to be doing heavy track work, it'll be a worthy purchase. To make the launch even quicker, the Cadillac can also lock the front wheels to create a huge burnout that warms up the tires. There's no line lock on the M3. In terms of interior space, there is a notable difference. In the second row, the CT4-V Blackwing has 33.4 inches of legroom and 36.5 inches of headroom, while the BMW has 35.6 and 37.8 inches, respectively. The BMW also has more trunk space at 13 cubic feet, a sizable difference when it serves as your daily driver. Is that worth the price? We wouldn't say so, and if you're particularly concerned about space, you'd be better served by the BMW M5 and CT5-V instead. Something we haven't mentioned is the fact that while the BMW M3 will soldier on in 2027 and then further on with a new generation, the CT4-V's future hangs in the balance. It has been officially discontinued after 2026, and GM has not released many details about its successor. All we currently know is that its larger sibling, the CT5-V, will return as a gas-powered sedan in the near future. Order books are currently closed for the CT4, although some inventory remains. The BMW might have the name, the history, and the more in-your-face design, but the more affordable Cadillac is definitely not far behind. With similar features and more affordable options, we'd recommend the CT4-V Blackwing to anyone looking for a capable daily driver. If you're chasing absolute performance, the M3's more powerful sibling with a Competition badge might be better for you – but the base model looks overpriced parked next to its American rival. While many say BMW's best M3 came in the 2000s, Cadillac's sports sedans only get better, and that will help the CT4-V's resale value down the road. Given Cadillac's F1 team, the special plaque inside the vehicle with the VIN number, and the fact it may be the last small performance sedan for a while, there's a good chance that it will come out on top of the BMW M3 in a few years. In our research, we could only find a few listings for the current and previous model year, and all are selling for more than the car's base price. Given the car's slowing sales toward the end of its life, these will probably be the most valuable in a couple of years, although early models can be found for just under $50,000. With GM's shift towards more electric vehicles, don't be surprised if the Cadillac stands as one of the last bastions of pure RWD sedan fun. We want to hear from you. Born April 19, 1935 in Westfield, MA, he attended Catholic school and went on to serve in the army, becoming a Korean War veteran. A longtime parishioner of St. Bernard’s Church, he was an accomplished runner, completing 84 marathons, including many Boston Marathon races, and races to the top of Mount Washington and countless challenging road races. He took pride in involving his children and grandchildren in his love of running, having them join him on the course for many years at races. His vocations included being a construction worker and a carpenter, as well as having worked in paper mills and in the maintenance department at local Catholic schools. He was a longtime devoted volunteer and board member for the North Medford Running Club. He also volunteered much time at St. Bernard’s church where he established a scholarship for students to be able to attend the St. Bernard High School. He was predeceased by his parents, Esther and Daniel McDermott; brothers Jim, Phil and Tom; his devoted wife Joan, who passed away earlier this year (and her parents, Joseph and Minnie Burdick); daughter, Judy and her longtime partner, Steve Robichaud; and his beautiful granddaughter, Heather Lynn. He is survived by his daughters Deb Fontaine and her husband Mark; Diane Rhoden and her husband, Rob; Brenda Fortier and her husband, Mark; son, Jim, and his wife, Brenda; daughter Karen Bergeron and her husband, Chuck; daughter, Susan Salazar. Additional survivors include his grandchildren, Alissa, Justin, Brittany, Mark Adam, Kaley, Katie, Stephanie, Lexi and Jen; great grandchildren, Everett, Wesley and Aiden; siblings, Cathy Mason, Peter, Matthew and Dan; numerous nieces and nephews, friends and running buddies. Calling hours will be held on Tuesday, August 4, 2026 at Richardson Funeral Home, 106 West St., Leominster, MA from 9:30-10:30 A.M. title: Tested: The Gas-Powered 2026 Honda CR-V Has Good Vibes, but Is the Hybrid Better? - MotorTrend
content: Honda’s stalwart SUV is as good as you remember, but the hybrid version is arguably the better buy. We know why you’re here, so we won’t bury the lede: Yes, the Honda CR-V is, in just about every meaningful way, still the same cheerful compact SUV that has established itself as a go-to purchase over three decades and six generations. The 2026 Honda CR-V EX-L AWD tested here is the most well-equipped gas-only model, with a price that places it smack in the middle of the CR-V lineup, above the gasoline LX and EX and the least expensive hybrid, the Sport. We liked the CR-V EX-L a lot—but is it good enough to be your next daily driver? Can this gas-only iteration make a case for itself against its competition, not to mention the hybrid CR-V in the same showroom? Let’s dig in. We’ll start with the basics of the EX-L AWD. For $38,805 as tested, you get a 1.5-liter, 190-hp turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a CVT automatic, and optional AWD. Leather-trimmed seats, a power tailgate, parking sensors, low-speed braking capability, eight-speaker sound, and an auto-dimming rearview mirror round out the EX-L’s light-luxury features. It’s cheaper than the hybrid CR-V’s entry-level Sport trim, but only slightly, with their base MSRPs just a few hundred dollars apart. The CR-V lineup got a comprehensive redesign for the 2023 model year, which brought a refined shape and such niceties as 18-inch wheels and wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto—but there’s not much you couldn’t get on, say, a decently optioned EX. Perhaps a look inward will reveal the EX-L’s value proposition. With its leather touches, the EX-L’s cabin is a bit nicer than lower-trim CR-Vs, but you won’t find yards of luxury materials or big infotainment screens here. Everything inside feels high quality, durable, and well assembled, though, and the 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen is perfectly adequate for tasks related to operating a motor vehicle and its basic functions. Its front-and-center placement on the dashboard keeps your head up and eyes in the general direction of the road, and its unique blend of hard buttons and touchscreen functionality works well. Likewise, the 10.2-inch driver display is, uh, somewhat spartan, with a couple of round, digitally rendered gauges and a small center readout for tracking things like cruise control status as its default state. It is customizable to a degree, but there’s just not enough room to change things up too much. We appreciate Honda’s resistance to unnecessarily large interfaces in the CR-V—in no small part, admittedly, because it necessitates old-school physical controls for basic functions like climate and audio, which we’re coming to regard as nonnegotiable. Honda Sensing, Honda’s suite of driver assists, is included in every CR-V. It provides pre-collision braking, throttle control, and steering functions, as well as lane keeping, adaptive cruise control with Traffic Jam Assist, adaptive headlights, parking sensors, and cross traffic monitoring, among many other features. We found the adaptive cruise and traffic jam functions especially useful, though several times we noted an uncomfortable abruptness to the system’s braking in traffic, which might make us think twice about using it a lot. We found nothing uncomfortable about the CR-V EX-L’s perforated-leather-trimmed seats, though. Both rows are roomy and supportive, with plenty of legroom for front and rear passengers. The EX-L gets four-way power front seats, and for 2026 both rows get charging capability, with a wireless phone charger, USB-A, and USB-C for the folks up front and two USB-C ports for the rear passengers. Cargo space is one place the gas-only CR-V may have the hybrids beat—because it doesn’t have the same drivetrain componentry to package, the gas variant enjoys 3 extra cubic feet behind the second row, for a total of 39.3. There’s plenty of cargo room with the rear seats up and quite a bit more when you fold them. With rear seats up or down, the CR-V EX-L’s cargo volume beats the Toyota RAV-4, Subaru Forester, and Nissan Rogue, too. Overall, the CR-V’s ergonomics and layout feel familiar, with controls that are thoughtfully laid out and excellent outward visibility—in short, all the things that make getting into a 2026 CR-V like slipping on an old sweater are in evidence. You’ll have to decide whether that’s a desirable quality or not. With a turbocharged, direct-injected 1.5-liter I-4 engine pushing 190 horsepower and 179 lb-ft of torque through a CVT automatic, the AWD CR-V EX-L went from 0 to 60 mph in 8.4 seconds in our testing, which makes it a tad slow for the broader segment. Notably, it’s also slower than it used to be. In 2026, the CR-V’s natural enemy, the Toyota RAV4, can get to 60 mph more than a second quicker at minimum, but with a big caveat to bear in mind: All RAV4s are now hybrids. A 2025 RAV4 with the now-retired gas powertrain needed around eight seconds, and the newly redesigned gas Mazda CX-5 needed 8.8 seconds to get to 60 mph in our testing. And the CR-V hybrid? It’s right on the RAV4, with a 0–60-mph time of about 7.5 seconds. All that being said, though, our gas CR-V didn’t feel especially slow. From a stop and when hitting the accelerator from low speeds, it exhibited little of the throttle lag or surging that often plagues vehicles with small turbocharged engines. It revs like a Honda should, but it does so linearly, smoothly, and without drama, in part thanks to its CVT transmission, which feels as much like a traditional automatic as you could reasonably expect. That’s only part of what makes the 2026 CR-V an unexpected pleasure to drive, though. Its brakes have surprisingly good feel for a vehicle of this kind, with decent bite and a pedal that accurately translates what’s going on at the wheels. Handling is similarly pleasing. The term “carlike” gets throw around a lot in regard to small SUVs, but in this case, it’s apt; the CR-V isn’t a canyon-carver, but we think its cornering, AWD grip, and general sense of composure and stability make it above average for the segment—even, dare we say, a little bit fun. Steering feel did leave something to be desired, though. Also leaving something to be desired is the gas CR-V’s fuel economy. We realized about 26 mpg average in our time with the SUV, good for a driving range in the neighborhood of 364 miles—significantly less than the official rating of 27/31/29 mpg city/highway/combined should yield. AWD doesn’t help matters, but as you’d expect, the hybrid variants trounce the gas CR-Vs in this regard, even when identically equipped—the most efficient AWD hybrid gets 40/34 mpg city/highway and 518 miles of range, and even the least efficient hybrid variant, the new TrailSport, gets 38/33 mpg and can go nearly 500 miles between fill-ups. If you’re thinking it sounds like the CR-V is behind the times, we can’t argue with you—but that may be one of its greatest selling points. It neither overwhelms nor underwhelms; it’s a totally familiar, even comforting experience while managing to offer some driver engagement. It’s easy to see what makes this vehicle the default for so many buyers, year after year. If you want the nicest gas-only 2026 CR-V you can get, you’ll find little to regret about the EX-L. If you’re looking for maximum value and the most traditional CR-V experience, though, the second-tier EX or even the base LX may offer enough for thousands less than the EX-L. And while we’re at it, unless you’re allergic to orange accents, we think the Sport Hybrid, which starts within a few hundred dollars of the EX-L but offers superior power and efficiency and comparable amenities, is worthy of serious consideration. Whatever flavor you choose, though, it’s tough to go wrong with a Honda CR-V. Get the newest car reviews, hottest auto news, and expert analysis of the latest trends delivered straight to your inbox! The Greek government has approved a €3.5 billion defense procurement package as part of a long-term program to modernize the country’s armed forces. Through this decision, Greece will acquire an Israeli air and missile defense system. According to Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias, a key element of the package will be the creation of the Achilles Shield multilayered air and missile defense system to protect against ballistic missiles and drones, Ekathimerini reported. The system will be based on Israeli radars and interceptors, while Greece’s defense industry will contribute around €700 million to its implementation. The government also approved the purchase of Heron 1 unmanned aircraft systems, 10 V-BAT Class II drones, and SAR satellites. For the Hellenic Navy and special operations forces, Greece will acquire countermeasures against uncrewed surface vessels and 10 special underwater vehicles. The package also includes funding to modernize four Hydra-class (MEKO 200HN) frigates with advanced anti-submarine warfare systems. The air component will be strengthened with three Embraer C-390 Millennium military transport aircraft under an intergovernmental agreement with Portugal. The package also includes the purchase of AGM-114 Hellfire air-to-ground missiles for AH-64 Apache attack helicopters and night vision equipment for infantry units. In addition to equipment purchases, funding will be allocated to train Greek officers in the United States in autonomous systems and artificial intelligence. The second phase of the defense program for 2027–2037, which will include the acquisition of F-35 fighter jets and new frigates, will be presented in September. Earlier this year, the Greek Parliament’s Armaments Committee approved the procurements. title: James V. Hebert - InForum
content:
James V. Hebert was born on September 20, 1935, in Fargo, ND to Leon and Rose (Fugere) Hebert, the second son in a family of eight children. (He is survived by Louise Lingen of Perham, MN and predeceased by Genevieve Durben, Marie Haugen, Eileen Cossette, Willard Hebert, Carol Hebert, and Shirley England.) While still in high school, James was accepted into the United States Marine Corps and served until 1957 when he was released from active duty as a motor man and transferred to the Marine Corps Reserve in Las Vegas, NV. He was honorably discharged in March of 1962. While serving his country, James completed high school, attained the rank of corporal and received the National Defense Service Medal. After military service, James made his home in Long Beach, CA, working for the US Postal Service in a 26-year career and retiring in 2002. Jimmy typically had a side hustle in play – such as working for the Los Angeles Rams football team, betting at the races or discovering a myriad of treasures and trinkets at garage sales. After retiring, James returned to live in Fargo. With religious devotion a consistent thread in his later life, Jimmy attended mass and services around the city. If you knew James, invariably you saw him with a newspaper in his pocket. He was a whiz with crossword puzzles and loved words. The art of song, poetry and elaborate story telling were Jimmy’s regular companions. All who knew him will recall his embellished holiday messages and greetings. James was generous in his unique way, always carrying silver coins or two-dollar bills to give or an offering from his eclectic garage sale collection. James’ checkbook was filled with entries of the many charities he supported, including and especially organizations of ministry and the Catholic Church. title: Opening the Door to Pool Determination: Tesla v InterDigital and Avanci - Wolters Kluwer
content: Opening the Door to Pool Determination: Tesla v InterDigital and Avanci The UK Supreme Court has considered the fundamental principles of (F)RAND, this time in the context of a jurisdiction challenge in Tesla v InterDigital and Avanci. In what could prove to be a significant shake-up in the FRAND world, in a decision dated 27 July 2026, the UK Supreme Court allowed Tesla’s appeal and thus opened the door to potential pool-rate setting actions in the UK in the future. In December 2023, Tesla started proceedings in the UK against InterDigital (a major licensor of the Avanci 5G Platform) and Avanci (the administrator of the platform, which does not own any SEPs itself). As part of these proceedings, Tesla sought declarations from the English Patents Court regarding the Avanci 5G Platform, including that a FRAND licence to InterDigital’s UK SEPs would be a global licence to the entire Avanci 5G Platform. Tesla also sought a declaration that the Avanci 5G Platform itself was not FRAND and a declaration as to what the FRAND rate would be. Together, these are known as “the Licensing Claims”. There was a jurisdiction challenge in 2024 where the Patents Court held that there was no serious issue to be tried on the Licensing Claims against InterDigital and Avanci. This was appealed to the Court of Appeal, where the majority dismissed Tesla’s appeal, with Lord Justice Arnold (a very experienced patents judge) dissenting. In a judgment given by Lord Hamblen and Lord Kitchin, and with which the other Justices of the Supreme Court agreed, the Supreme Court split this overarching question into three distinct sub-issues: On the first sub-issue, the Supreme Court considered the cases that Tesla had advanced. First, Tesla’s “extreme” contention was that a SEP owner is under an obligation to make sure that all its offers are on FRAND terms including to both bilateral and platform licences. Alternatively, the SEP owner remains bound by the FRAND obligation regardless of whether it makes an offer on a bilateral basis or via a pool or platform. Tesla’s position on this alternative was that, in circumstances where a SEP owner licenses through a pool or platform, it may be the case that only the pool or platform licence is FRAND. The Supreme Court considered that the common element of Tesla’s cases was that the SEP owner would remain bound by the FRAND obligation even if licensing through a pool or platform. Considering the wording of the ETSI FRAND obligation, the drafting of the obligation in conjunction with the European Commission (and thus the importance of competition policy), and the general policy justification where over 90% of the stack was offering its patents through the platform, the Supreme Court held that there is a serious issue to be tried as to whether the FRAND obligation applies to offers made through a platform. On the second sub-issue, the Supreme Court commented that it did not find Telsa’s “extreme” formulation of its case to be persuasive.  Rather the FRAND obligation requires SEP owners to ensure that FRAND terms are available, but it does not preclude them from negotiating different commercial but non-FRAND terms.  In finding that there was a serious issue to be tried here too, the Court again pointed to the commercial realities of the market and the impracticalities of implementers bilaterally licensing with every SEP-owner in the platform. In particular, it noted that most licensors to the Avanci 5G Platform rely on it as meeting their FRAND obligation, and noted the impracticality of seeking bilateral licences to every licensor in the platform. In assessing this issue, the Supreme Court made clear that this is not a requirement for SEP holders to join a platform and offer their SEPs via that platform, and it recognised the commercial freedom of a particular SEP holder to join or leave a platform as it sees fit. However, the core issue related to a SEP holder which is a member of the platform, so there was a serious issue to be tried. The third sub-issue required the Supreme Court to determine whether Tesla had a real prospect of being granted the declarations sought against both InterDigital and Avanci. After a review of the Court’s declaratory powers and the circumstances in which these should be exercised, the Supreme Court considered that the declarations sought against InterDigital were based on a real and present dispute stemming from InterDigital’s FRAND obligation. For Avanci, the Supreme Court found that it was not necessary for Tesla to have a cause of action against Avanci, so long as there was a useful purpose. The Supreme Court considered that Tesla had a real prospect of showing that the declarations it sought served a useful purpose. In particular, if a declaration was to be made that the FRAND rate for the Avanci 5G Platform was less than that on offer, Avanci would likely reconsider its position. The Supreme Court also considered that, if such declarations were not available, this would seriously undermine the effectiveness of the FRAND regime, as there could be no possibility of court scrutiny of a pool or platform rate. The Supreme Court also considered that there was no procedural unfairness associated with granting the declarations. It noted that Avanci was the “essential party” in any court determination of the Avanci 5G Platform licence and other licensors in the platform would be able to apply to join proceedings should they so wish. The Supreme Court considered the “formidable line of authority” which has developed in the UK since the Vestel case and found that the Licensing Claims were properly characterised as a licensing claim relating to UK SEPs. Therefore, the Supreme Court found that the Licensing Claims were properly served on InterDigital Patent Holdings according to CPR r.63.14, which allows service on the address registered with the UK IPO for the relevant UK patents. The claims also passed through the relevant “gateways” for service out of the jurisdiction. In particular, the Licensing Claims passed through: The Supreme Court considered whether the Delaware Court of Chancery was a more appropriate forum to hear the dispute than the UK. It held that it would not be more appropriate, as the Delaware Court of Chancery would only adjudicate FRAND terms for US patents and not for UK patents. It is important to note that this is not a finding by the Supreme Court that pool or platform administrators are subject to the FRAND obligation, nor is it a finding that the only FRAND licence available to a particular licensor’s SEPs must be the global platform licence. The Supreme Court has only held that there are serious issues to be tried on these points, and those issues will now go back to the Patents Court to be decided on the merits. So this is likely not the end of the story. © 2025 Wolters Kluwer N.V. and/or its subsidiaries. All rights reserved.

title: 2026 Honda CR-V EX-L vs. 2026 Mazda CX-5 Premium Plus Tested: Which Compact SUV Is Better? - Car and Driver
content:
The CX-5 and CR-V are both longtime Car and Driver favorites, but with the Mazda fully redesigned for 2026, which one comes out on top? Let's make a bet. Head over to your well-lit display case (or back closet) stacked full of old Car and Driver issues, dust off any 10Best issue from the last decade or so, and we'd wager that either the Honda CR-V or Mazda CX-5 is on that list. With nine of the 10 most recent 10Best lists containing either the Honda or the Mazda, it's clear that the two models are perennial favorites around our office—and, according to sales figures, around the country. Since Mazda gave the CX-5 a full redesign for 2026, we figured it was a good time to get these two longtime favorites together for a bit of friendly competition. Much like a Burger King order, the 2026 Honda CR-V can be had your way. The lineup starts with the LX at $32,370, which is powered by a 190-hp turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-four, and is available in front- or all-wheel drive. If you're looking for a bit more power, a few more features, or better fuel economy, the CR-V's got you covered with an entire lineup of hybrids. We tested a 2026 EX-L, the top trim for nonhybrid CR-Vs, starting at $36,850; the all-wheel drive and optional Radiant Red Metallic paint push its as-tested price to $38,805. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V for sale and new 2026 Mazda CX-5 for sale near 85032 Currently, Mazda's CX-5 stable contains just one powertrain, although a hybrid model is slated to arrive for 2027. Every 2026 CX-5, including our Premium Plus test model, comes equipped with a 187-hp 2.5-liter inline-four, and all-wheel drive is standard. The CX-5's price band is a bit broader than the Honda's, starting at $31,485 and rising all the way to $40,485, with our test example coming in at $41,080 with its extra-cost Aero Gray Metallic paint. Whether you see Honda's interior design as a positive or a negative is up to you, but the fact is, the design works. The CR-V's interior is roomy and easy to see out of. The materials—at least in our EX-L—are high-quality and comfortable to the touch even if they don't impress much beyond that. The layout is simple, with 9.0 inches of infotainment screen acreage to provide you with what you need, but not enough to overwhelm. Climate controls are fuss-free. Want it warmer? Turn that obviously placed dial on the dashboard to the right. Is your butt a little cold? Don't worry, the heated seat button is placed well within arm's reach. Can't quite hear the music over the sound of your own singing? You've got physical controls on the steering wheel and infotainment screen ready to pump up the volume. HIGHS: Smart interior layout, hugely practical, confidence-inspiring dynamics. LOWS: Noisy cabin, lacks any premium feel, could be quicker. VERDICT: Easy to love, hard to hate. Mazda's interior, on the other hand, goes all in on digital controls. The new-generation CX-5 places just about every non-driving function, from volume to vehicle settings, on the 15.6-inch dash-mounted do-it-all touchscreen. So long as you're cool with this approach, the CX-5's interior impresses. The seats, doors, and dashboard all sport leather wrappings, and the new "Mazda" script on the steering wheel evokes thoughts of luxury goods. Sitting in the CX-5, you're met with a cozy space that feels more premium than what's in the Honda, but we can't help noticing that the refreshed car doesn't seem quite as upscale as the older version. See all results for new 2026 Honda CR-V for sale and new 2026 Mazda CX-5 for sale near 85032 The CR-V's airy cabin puts a premium on passenger space and narrowly edges the CX-5 in rear-seat room—this despite the Honda having a shorter wheelbase: 106.3 inches to the Mazda's 110.8. In compact SUVs, storage space is as important as passenger comfort, and the CR-V wins there as well, offering 39 cubic feet behind the rear seats and 77 cubic feet with the seats folded. The CX-5 has 34 cubic feet behind the rear seats and only improves to 67 cubic feet with the rear seats laid flat. From an exterior-design perspective, we prefer the CX-5. Both models are reasonably handsome, but the Mazda's muscular lines and swoopy roofline evoke a bit more emotion, while the CR-V's aging design feels a tad more mundane. Should the two ever enter a drag race together, the result would be close. Despite the CX-5's extra 262 pounds, its 8.3-second run to 60 mph matches that of the lighter CR-V. The Mazda noses ahead in the quarter-mile, beating the Honda by 0.1 second, although the CR-V's 3-mph-higher trap speed shows the Honda is pulling harder by the end. That continues beyond the quarter-mile, where the CR-V reaches 100 mph 2.4 seconds sooner than the CX-5. Champagne for the winner, even if it is by the slimmest of margins. HIGHS: Superior ride quality, quieter cruising, more stylish looks. LOWS: "Everything's computer," ho-hum fuel economy, higher price. VERDICT: Still great but slips a little with this redesign. Honda did an admirable job tuning the CR-V's continuously variable automatic transmission to reduce that tech's worst attributes, but nothing beats the real thing, which is what you get in the Mazda. Urge the CX-5 to accelerate for a pass on the highway, and the six-speed automatic transmission kicks down to provide extra power for the task. And against the stopwatch, the Mazda beat the Honda in our 50-to-70-mph highway passing test by two-tenths. Despite that, the CR-V feels reasonably peppy. Give the throttle a good stab, and the Honda responds. Tell the CX-5 to accelerate, and it's got a hair more urgency than the CR-V, although the engine feels and sounds a bit less refined in doing so. The CR-V's small-displacement engine is efficient, earning EPA estimates of 27 mpg in the city and 31 mpg on the highway. That beats the CX-5's numbers, which are 24 mpg in the city and 30 mpg on the highway. Our test CR-V's observed fuel economy came in at 25 mpg; we don't yet have results for the CX-5 in that same test. At a steady 70 mph, the Mazda is noticeably quieter than the Honda. The former measures at just 23 sones, while the latter lets in more wind and road noise at 26 sones, or some 13 percent louder. However, the Mazda's coarse powertrain is more vocal under acceleration, measuring at 77 decibels to the Honda's 74 at wide-open throttle. Still, settle into a cruise on the highway, and either cabin becomes a quiet enough place to happily spend your commute. Leave your daily drive behind, and both cars are considerably more athletic than they need to be. The CR-V drives like most Hondas, with nicely weighted steering that has a solid on-center feel. The Honda has a touch more body roll than the Mazda, but unless you're driving them back to back, you'd be hard-pressed to notice the difference. The CX-5 is similarly dynamic. The steering has more of an artificial feel than the Honda's, but it provides confidence-inspiring feedback and a clear sense of on-center. We prefer the CX-5's softer ride to the CR-V's slightly stiffer one. Neither beats you up over bumps, but the Honda jolts you a bit more, especially over sharp impacts. The CR-V takes the crown thanks mostly to its easier-to-use interior, additional usable space, and its lower price. That's not to say the CX-5 isn't a contender. It's got solid dynamics, and it looks great—as long as you don't mind the screen-centric interior design. Furthermore, the Honda's more efficient powertrain and lower starting price make the CR-V the thriftier option up front and going forward. And in this segment, practicality counts.
