title: 2025 Honda CR-V Owner Drives a 2026 Toyota RAV4 450 Miles, Hits 44.5 MPG, But Still Refuses to Buy One Over a Key Interior Flaw - Torque News
content:
That is real-world hybrid efficiency at its absolute peak. Yet, one long-term Honda owner is walking away from Toyota's crown jewel. When St. Louis resident Yvan Carr-Chua handed back the keys to a 2026 Toyota RAV4 loaner after logging 450 miles across Missouri interstates, rural highways, and surface streets, he was staring at a massive mathematical victory. His personal vehicle, a 2025 Honda CR-V Sport Hybrid, averages 33.8 MPG over 22,000 miles of daily driving, meaning the rival RAV4 handed him a staggering 10.7 MPG jump without a single change to his driving style. Despite that insane 600-mile range on a single 14-gallon tank, Carr-Chua is stubbornly refusing to jump ship to Toyota, exposing a major hidden rift in the compact SUV wars that window stickers completely fail to capture. As I have noted in my investigative analysis on Toyota RAV4 Hybrid vs. Honda CR-V Hybrid: There's Only One That Will Last 300,000 Miles, while Toyota’s planetary gear e-CVT architecture remains an absolute mechanical vault for ultra-high-mileage drivers, Honda’s cabin ergonomics present an entirely different level of daily refinement that legacy specs cannot measure. In a candid breakdown shared on the Honda CR-V 2023-2026 Facebook Discussion Club, Carr-Chua delivered an unvarnished owner-to-owner comparison that cuts straight to the root cause of why fuel economy alone no longer guarantees brand loyalty. “I’m currently in a 2026 RAV4 rental for the week and here’s my takeaway as a 2025 CR-V Sport Hybrid owner... Exterior: By far the best-looking RAV4 they’ve put out. Interior: Meh… same old song and dance from Toyota. If somewhat rugged, somewhat childproof, and lots of plastic is your vibe, then this is the vehicle for you. The lines feel dated, the cuts aren’t luxurious, and the materials are lackluster... Infotainment greatly outclasses the CR-V... Fuel Economy: If this is your top item, I’ve never seen anything like this... I’m getting 44.5 mpg with zero adjustment to my driving style at all! Holy crap. 600 miles to a 14-gallon tank is insane... In conclusion, I personally would not purchase one, as I’m loyal to Honda, and prefer the nicer interior design.” That single assessment highlights the exact tactical tradeoff drivers are silently making on dealership lots across North America today. A comprehensive multi-vehicle comparative report from U.S. News & World Report Automotive Division notes that "the cabin quality, with its high-end materials and user-friendly technology, gives the interior a finish that reflects Honda's consistent investment in the tactile quality of its most accessible models." Why does a buyer willingly forfeit nearly 11 extra miles per gallon just to stay inside a Honda? The root cause isn't found on a standard brochure; it resides deep within the structural assembly and material science of modern vehicle dashboards. Toyota deliberately engineers the RAV4’s interior around hard, high-durability polypropylene plastics to lower manufacturing overhead, meet strict fleet durability targets, and provide a "childproof" cabin that resists severe scratches over a decade of abuse. However, those rigid plastic panels lack the acoustic damping layers and micro-foam backings that Honda integrates into the sixth-generation CR-V’s honeycomb dash architecture and isolated structural subframes. When you drive over expansion joints at 70 mph, those hard plastic cutouts in the Toyota transmit high-frequency vibration directly into the cabin, creating what Carr-Chua described as a "clunky dash cluster placed along a flat, water slide of a plastic dashboard." As I revealed in another field investigation, Honda CR-V Hybrid Owner Rents 2026 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, Rejects Its High Seating Position and Rough Ride Quality, Honda achieves its buttery acoustic advantage by utilizing a specialized, lightweight aluminum front subframe that is completely rubber-isolated from the primary unibody chassis. Industry-wide metric tracking from independent review groups like Ralph Honda Technical Analysis further confirms that while Toyota leans heavily into a rugged aesthetic, "the RAV4’s entry-level and mid-tier trims feature practical interior materials that do not match the sophisticated tactile experience and premium leather-wrapped touchpoints engineered into the CR-V.” Rocky Mountain Altitude Testing Exposes The Real-World MPG Gap Living and testing vehicles here in Parker, Colorado, I regularly push these hybrid crossovers through severe elevation swings, sub-zero morning cold starts, and steep mountain passes along the Front Range. High-altitude atmospheric changes expose a fascinating engineering split between these two automotive giants. Toyota’s 2.5-liter naturally aspirated Atkinson-cycle engine paired with its dual-electric motor setup relies on aggressive engine RPM flare under load, which allows the engine to generate massive efficiency sweet spots on flat Midwest terrain—explaining Carr-Chua’s insane 44.5 MPG run in Missouri. However, up here at 6,000+ feet above sea level, that same Toyota powertrain screams loudly under hard acceleration, vibrating through that hard plastic dashboard and disrupting the peace of the cabin. Honda’s two-motor direct-drive hybrid powertrain operates more like an electric vehicle, using its 2.0-liter gas engine primarily as an onboard generator, which keeps cabin decibel levels significantly lower during high-stress mountain climbs. While Colorado drivers might see their fuel economy drop closer to the 34 MPG mark due to thin air and steep gradients, the acoustic insulation of the CR-V creates a calm, luxury-adjacent environment that hard plastic utility vehicles simply cannot replicate. If Toyota clearly dominates the raw mileage test while Honda wins the cabin refinement battle, which hybrid setup actually survives long-term mechanical abuse without throwing catastrophic diagnostic trouble codes? The immediate answer boils down to your regional climate and long-term ownership goals. If you live in a snowy, road-salt state where high-voltage corrosion is a constant threat, Honda’s simplified direct-drive hybrid transmission eliminates the vulnerable rear high-voltage harness layout that has plagued older RAV4 models. Conversely, if you live in a dry climate, drive 30,000 miles annually, and view your crossover purely as a tool to haul kids and gear, Toyota's bulletproof planetary gear train will easily march to 300,000 miles long after the plastic interior trim has aged. Yvan Carr-Chua’s week-long test proves that vehicle purchasing decisions are no longer decided by a single impressive stat line on a window sticker. Toyota built an incredible fuel-sipping powertrain wrapped in a rugged appliance, but Honda built a cohesive, comfortable daily sanctuary that owners simply enjoy sitting in every single morning. title: Alvin V. Drake, 73 - The Laconia Daily Sun
content:
MEREDITH — Alvin Vernal Drake, son of Vernal and Janet Drake, passed away on July 2, 2026, at home in Meredith. Alvin was born in Laconia, on June 4, 1953, and grew up in New Hampton, with his five siblings, Susan Allen (husband Peter) of Gilford, Linda Normandin (husband Paul, predeceased) of Belmont, Brenda Moynihan (husband Keith) of Charlotte, North Carolina, Betty Bilodeau (husband Guy) of Manchester, and William Drake of Gaffney, South Carolina. He graduated from Newfound Memorial High School in 1971. Alvin was proud of this three sons, Jacob Drake of Thornton, Michael Drake of Savanah, Georgia, and Daniel Drake of Windham, Maine. He treasured the time he was able to spend with his two grandsons, Roo and Wilder. He was a true craftsman and skilled woodsman, much of which was learned from his father. Alvin had the ability to craft all the lumber for his house from his own land. He cut the trees and shaped them into the size he needed. They were then sent off to the kiln. When returned, he cut and sized them to build his house. He was proud to tell you exactly what tree each piece of lumber in his house came from. He had a beautiful workshop with every tool needed to complete the job. Alvin passed on his skills to his son Jacob, who continues to work in the construction business. title: Tested: 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S680 V-12 Delivers Old-World Opulence - Road & Track
content: Nobody needs a V-12. But the top Maybach version of the S-Class makes an excellent case for still wanting one. No matter the form, Maybach’s take on the Mercedes S-Class is not for the sort of person worried about the optics of arriving in style. For the past decade, Maybach has been turned into a theater of opulence. Over the top is the whole point, with the Maybach logo as prominent on some cars as the Louis Vuitton emblem on hugely expensive bags. So it makes sense that Maybach goes one step further. The V-8-powered Maybach S580 is there if you want it, and any rational person probably should, but the ultraluxury-sedan buyer is rarely rational. For those who demand the most Maybach version of a Maybach sedan, the S680 still packs 12 cylinders of silky-smooth urge under its elegant hood. Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here. The 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S680 is, as its name implies, positioned about 100 points of badge better than the S580. The key distinction here is a twin-turbocharged V-12 that can trace its origins back over 20 years. The rest will look familiar, from the traditional three-pointed star hanging atop the massive front grille to the light-up Maybach wordmark below it. V-12 aside, the centerpiece is still the air suspension, Airmatic in Mercedes-Benz parlance, that is in this application aided by tech that scans the road to adjust the system for whatever it faces next. Despite having 50 percent more capacity and cylinders than the V-8 S580, the range topper’s power output is not correspondingly higher. The S680 makes relaxed peaks of 621 hp and 664 lb-ft, those figures being 91 hp and 111 lb-ft higher than the corresponding ones for the smaller-engine car. Mercedes claims identical 4.3-second 0–60-mph times for both cars. But numbers will only ever be a small part of the story for cars like this. Transmission: Nine-speed automatic, all-wheel drive EPA Fuel Economy: 12 mpg city, 20 mpg highway, 14 mpg combined Many modern Mercedes products, AMG badged ones in particular, are harsh and explosive things. For the past decade, the company’s performance badge has been building all shapes and sizes of car that explode off the line with turbocharged power and stay flat under heavy cornering loads. The Maybach S680 does none of that. The twin-turbocharged V-12 produces a superabundance of torque, but the 664 lb-ft delivers an effortlessness that makes it easy to experience acceleration that is both impressive and relaxing at the same time—satisfying an owner-driver behind the wheel but not disturbing them if they experienced the same forces while luxuriating in the back. Braking, too, mostly comes in the form of champagne stops, bringing the car to a rest without spilling a drop of a passenger’s drink. The S680 can stop itself in a hurry if it needs to, but the normal slowdown won’t disturb a sleeping occupant. In a world where powerful cars fight hard to defeat body roll and the once-sluggish response of automatic transmissions, the S680 is a throwback. It experiences noticeable lean under cornering loads, and it never feels responsive even in its sharpest Sport drive mode. The gearbox also decides to shift to its own agenda, rather than where a driver might expect it to. Rolls-Royce used to describe this sort of stately performance as “adequate,” and while the Maybach is capable of lifting its skirts in a way that old Rollers never could, the descriptor is still perfect for the way it delivers without ever seeming to break a sweat. Sure, it felt a little out of place on a quick run up and down the famous Angeles Crest Highway, a road with as many corners as straights. But any buyer looking for an S-Class to excel in that situation would most likely opt for the S63 AMG version. The Maybach is nobody’s one-car performance solution; it’s an ultraluxurious product designed to waft along the road in style. Materials are spectacular, particularly at this price point, which is well below what you’d pay for a similarly optioned Bentley or Rolls-Royce product. This is nobody’s idea of a subtle car, but those worried about the perceived stealthy nature of an ultraluxury sedan based on a mere luxury sedan can make their S680 stand out with a wide array of options from Mercedes’s Manufaktur range. That list includes more than 50 unique colors or combinations, plus a couple of dozen leather finishes. Buyers looking for something even more exclusive can head to the new Made to Measure studio in Los Angeles to spec a car from hundreds of individual options. The red interior optioned on the car I tested was certainly striking. Plenty of the two-tone options that have become a hallmark of Maybach offerings are available, including this far-from-subtle black and dark gray metallic pairing that could arguably stand to be a little bit more ostentatious. The key option is a $6000 Executive Rear Seat package. This drops the middle seat and all the compromises that come with it, leaving room for an $1100 refrigerated rear center console and a $3200 set of silver-plated champagne flutes. Those options might not exactly be a must, but the reclining right-rear seat is a particularly special place made all the more spectacular by the car’s impressive Burmester sound system. Buyers choosing the S680 for the noises its turbocharged V-12 produces may be disappointed to learn that excellent sound dampening kept things quiet throughout the cabin. This is a good thing, though; more than anything else, that peace and control over the environment inside the car is what makes an ultraluxury car feel special. The hallmark of the V-8 car, the Mercedes-Maybach S580, is that it is the standout bargain in the ultraluxury-sedan segment. The extra sum of cash to buy the V-12 moves the S680 back toward the range of the Bentley Flying Spur, an all-time great car that is significantly better at the performance tasks the Maybach intentionally ignores. Still, this car starts at a lower number and should typically come out to be less expensive after being optioned to a similar level. Plus it has a V-12, whereas the Spur has a hybridized V-8. The Rolls-Royce Ghost has 12 cylinders, but it also costs over $100,000 more. The S680 comes with the key advantage of sitting at the very top of the Maybach pecking order. This is the car people think of when they say the name, the closest thing to a successor to the 57 and 62 sedans that relaunched the brand for 2003. Wearing the two-tone paint that best shows off the massively extended rear doors that come with the 7.1-inch wheelbase stretch over the standard S-Class, the Maybach S680 manages to look the proverbial million dollars at what’s nearly a 75 percent discount. For the buyers Mercedes is targeting, the massive presence is a huge selling point. That leaves one major question: Why opt for the V-12 over the V-8? The extra torque certainly helps move the hefty sedan in effortless comfort, sure, but the real answer might be even more simple—for some, bigger will always be better. As happy as we are to see the V-12 live for another generation, the S680’s advantages over the S580 are more emotional than rational. But if you’re going to buy a Maybach, wouldn’t you want it to be the best one? Lounge-style rear seating is a must for anyone optioning out a car like this, and the Maybach team has a strong understanding of how to make that space feel special. With the seat fully reclined, massage functions active, and chilled champagne in those ridiculous logo-adorned silver flutes, a properly equipped S680 is rolling serenity. But this time out, we decided to largely play chauffer instead and experience the hand-built V-12 from behind the wheel in a variety of settings, everything from sweeping curves to traffic-choked highways to packed city streets. The 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S-Class will be offered in two variants for the U.S. market: the S580 and S680. The S580 uses a version of Benz's newly revised twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 mild hybrid powertrain producing 530 hp and 553 lb-ft of torque, while the S680 is propelled by a carryover version of the automaker's mighty twin-turbo 6.0-liter V-12 generating 621 hp and 664 lb-ft. Both engines are paired to a nine-speed automatic transmission that sends power to all four wheels through Mercedes' 4Matic all-wheel-drive system. Our drive route began on the busy streets of Beverly Hills, where escaping traffic was the first test of the day, one the Maybach handled with ease. We did notice a slight shudder when the engine's stop/start system restarted the V-12, something that was far less apparent in the mild hybrid V-8 model, which uses its e-motor largely as a starter-generator. Despite the traffic and the sedan's imposing 215.9-inch length, getting around Beverly Hills was surprisingly easy. The Maybach S680 is a genuinely big car, yet it never felt unwieldy when rolling down Rodeo Drive. Our test car's optional 21-inch wheels limited the rear-axle steering to 4.5 degrees, but the system still helped when negotiating tight corners and maneuvering into parking spaces. Once we reached freeway speeds, the ride became even more supple and the cabin quieter. Whatever little noise does intrude can be easily drowned out by the ridiculously impressive Burmester audio system with Dolby Atmos, which transforms the cabin into a private music studio. Malibu's tightest canyon roads are far from the S680's natural habitat, but along Kanan Dume Road's broad sweepers and steep climbs, the brawny sedan never felt challenged. It surged uphill and dispatched slower-moving vehicles with effortless authority. The 12-cylinder engine always has ample power in reserve, yet its linear delivery makes acceleration feel smooth and discreet. Press the accelerator harder, though, and all 621 horses come alive, propelling the Maybach with remarkable force. The ride quality is even more impressive, and it's here that the Maybach truly distinguishes itself from its lesser S-Class siblings. Our S680 was equipped with Maybach's intelligent damping system, which helps it shrug off pavement imperfections with ease. A couple of large undulations along our Malibu canyon route caused the cars ahead of us to bounce several times, but the S680 absorbed the same heaves in one controlled motion. Its chassis remained composed, and the disturbance barely registered inside the cabin. Although we spent most of our time behind the wheel, we couldn't help but pull over for a few minutes to sample the Maybach's phenomenal rear-seat setup. Once you settle into its plush, Nappa leather–swathed seats with their particularly soft throw pillows, cushiony headrests, and copious massage options, you may never want to climb back out. The latest version of Mercedes' MBUX rear-seat entertainment screens let passengers stream videos from Disney+ and YouTube, and a selection of games can help pass the time between meetings. Although we didn't sip any champagne, the optional refrigerator setup between the rear seats can keep a bottle chilled, and dedicated holders secure the silver-plated flutes while freeing your hands. A remote control lets passengers activate the seat massagers, adjust the climate settings, and operate the window shades for additional privacy. Recline the seat back and extend the leg rest, and you'll feel suitably pampered whether you're heading to an evening gala or an early-morning board meeting. The 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S680 looks imposingly baller from every angle, and it will make any CEO or captain of industry feel like all that hard work has finally paid off. The updated model is beginning to arrive in the U.S. at around a cool quarter million to start, which is roughly $3,000 more than the 2026 version. That modest increase is unlikely to negatively influence anyone seriously considering adding one to their fleet. For those who still believe 12 cylinders and first-class luxury belong together, few cars make the case as convincingly as the S680—no matter if you're chauffeuring yourself or being chauffeured. title: 😱 It was an error: IFAB confirms Argentina were favoured v Switzerland - Yahoo Sports
content: The International Football Association Board (IFAB) has determined that Breel Embolo’s sending-off during the 2026 World Cup quarterfinals was the result of a refereeing and VAR interpretation error. In the 72nd minute, with the score at 1-1, the Swiss forward went down after a challenge with Leandro Paredes. After initially booking the Argentine, Portuguese referee João Pinheiro reviewed the play on VAR for a possible “mistaken identity.” After watching the replay, he withdrew Paredes’ card and showed Embolo a second yellow for simulation, sending him off. In its recent circular, IFAB clarified that the technological tool could only intervene to identify the player who committed the foul, but not to reassess the nature of the play or call deception. title: Lexi Minetree: Hollywood’s Newest Gemini Vegetarian is Legally Blonde - V Magazine
content: The ‘Elle’ star sits down with V to talk role models, post-breakup glow-ups, and reimagining the iconic Elle Woods The ‘Elle’ star sits down with V to talk role models, post-breakup glow-ups, and reimagining the iconic Elle Woods Before Elle Woods was a Zeta Lambda Nu sweetheart and president of Delta Nu with a bachelor’s degree in fashion merchandising and a diploma from Harvard Law School, she was a teenager. Imagined by Laura Kittrell, the prequel to Legally Blonde finds Elle Woods as Seattle, Washington’s newest resident. Starring Lexi Minetree, Elle is a coming-of-age story set around the beloved, blonde Elle Woods. Minetree steps into the role bearing a positive attitude similar to Woods, with an excited energy surrounding her breakthrough role. She’s a doppelganger to the original Elle Woods, a young Reese Witherspoon, and has a dedication to the accurate portrayal of the adored character. Like Woods, she spent her undergrad in California. Minetree graduated from the University of Southern California and has been featured in supporting roles with Elle being her breakthrough role. In an interview with V, the budding actress shared her hopes for Elle, her strongest personal inspirations, and moments that felt surreal surrounding the project. Ailbhe Killalea: Elle Woods is such an iconic character; we all grew up with her as a role model. Who are some of your role models? Lexi Minetree: My Aunt Emily is one of my biggest role models…and dare I say friends. She is a generous human. She’s wonderful and lovely and someone who gives people grace. I think we all need someone like that in our lives. She’s also just so cultured and interesting. She’d hate that I’m saying this, but it’s true. She’ll say words that I immediately write down in my notes app cause I want to try and implement them in my own life: dithering, punctilious, raconteur to name a few. Like, wouldn’t I sound so smarty pants if I dropped the word “abstruce” in a conversation? She’s a novelist, and she was a curator for a museum before. I’m always in awe of people who really understand the culture of the world and are constantly immersing themselves in it. She sees the world in a beautiful way. My little brother is also a role model of mine. He has Down syndrome, but I rarely see him upset about his disability. He just loves the world. He can make friends with anyone. We call him “the mayor” because every time he walks into a room, he just dazzles everyone. AK: I saw the video where you found out you got the role. What did that moment feel like? LM: It was very surreal, and honestly, it didn’t even feel real. When something that huge happens, it takes a while to process it. I got really lucky because they didn’t announce it until the next day, so I had about 24 hours to really take it all in and appreciate that all my hard work had paid off. I was so excited to dive into this character, and then I got really nervous because I was like, “Oh my God, this is going to be a lot.” But I was just excited to jump in and see what was going to happen next. Eek! AK: What part of Elle’s life/personality are you most excited for people to see in the new prequel? What do you think people misunderstand about Elle’s story? LM: I’m most excited for people to see her vulnerability and her having to learn in real time. I think especially in high school, we’re all traversing uncharted waters, and Elle is no exception. She really is another fish out of water in this story. I think something people might misunderstand is that growth is never a straight line. I’ve seen people wondering, “How can she go through the same struggle multiple times?” Or, “Why should we get invested in these relationships if we know they’re not going to matter later?” But I actually think that’s what makes it feel so real. Personally, progress has never been a straight line for me. It’s always been a bumpy road. It’s like the game Chutes and Ladders—sometimes you hit a ladder and shoot up, and sometimes you hit a slide and go all the way down. There are many relationships from my past I no longer interact with but that doesn’t shake the indelible impact they’ve had on my life. In Legally Blonde, Elle is already so confident. She’s this force, and everyone else is kind of catching up to her. She’s someone who is unequivocally kind to people, even people who aren’t kind to her, but she also has a little bite to her. I think what’s so fun about the prequel is that you get to see where all of those things come from and how she grows into them. AK: I actually grew up in Seattle and regularly wore a hot pink Juicy tracksuit to my private Catholic school. Looking back, it was both ridiculous and totally amazing. What about Seattle drew the story to relocate there? How does stepping outside of Southern California further develop the character of Elle Woods? LM: DIVAAAA!!!! First of all, you’re my hero, and I feel like we’d be friends. That is absolutely incredible. I hope your classmates thought you were an icon too. I think Elle Woods only exists as a fish out of water. You need to see her out of herELLEment—no pun intended. And I think putting her in Seattle during the grunge movement was perfect. Laura Kittrell, the creator, was a genius for that because it really couldn’t be further from Elle Woods. Especially in high school, she’s been in this Bel Air bubble of privilege, and then she goes to this school where everyone is a little bit more nonconformist and against “the man.” Trying is almost uncool. So I think it’s really cool to see her navigate people who are basically her antithesis and figure out how to find a common language with them. AK: Did anyone tell you that you look like Reese Witherspoon prior to getting this role? The resemblance is uncanny. LM: It was kind of a shocking amount of times. I would say it started my junior year of high school, and random people would just come up to me and tell me I looked like her. I always took it as such a huge compliment because she’s obviously gorgeous. But I never, ever would have thought that I’d actually be playing her. AK: Reese Witherspoon is the blueprint. What kind of conversations did you have with her about the series? How do you hope to carry on her legacy as Elle Woods? LM: I was really lucky because Reese gave me so much trust with this character and let me take the reins when it came to creating the high school version of Elle. We obviously would message and talk about the core of what makes Elle Woods, Elle Woods. But I also think Reese saw something in me from the get-go that was already the essence of the character, and I just kind of honed that as the process went along. AK: Elle’s character arc in Legally Blonde was the ultimate post-breakup glow-up. What are your tips for glowing up after a breakup? They say hair tells a story, and hair holds memories. So when you change your hair, it kind of feels like you’re entering a new era. The first thing I did when I finished the press tour for season one was ask Rory, my hairdresser, to please-and-thank-you cut my bangs. I’ve done it enough times myself and instantly regretted my choices because I have no idea how to cut hair. So I thought, “I’m going to leave it to the professionals this time,” and he delivered. I’m obsessed with them. It felt like a good symbolic way of reclaiming my autonomy and being like, “You know what? This was such an incredible moment, and now I’m entering a new one.” We are using cookies to give you the best experience on our website. title: Before the Sensor: Filter Ordering and Self-Collision in Amsted Rail v. Squires - Patently-O
content:
The Federal Circuit has affirmed the cancellation of claims in Amsted Rail's railcar monitoring patent, along with the Board's refusal to let Amsted swap in substitute claims. Amsted Rail Co. v. Squires, No. 2025-1063 (Fed. Cir. July 24, 2026) (nonprecedential). U.S. Patent No. 10,137,915 covers sensor nodes and radios bolted onto freight cars to watch for derailments, damaged wheels, and overheating bearings. Claim 1 recites: ... (b) one or more sensors ... configured to measure accelerations of the railcar; and
(c) one or more filters configured to filter at least a portion of the accelerations ... Amsted argued the two elements as a sequence: measure first, filter second. But the panel held that the claim imposes no order, which opened the door to invalidating prior art. Both appeals were argued on June 1: this one and a companion covering two more Amsted patents, which the same panel disposed of on June 3 with a one word Rule 36 judgment. Ordering. A claim does not require its elements to operate in sequence unless the language, as a matter of logic or grammar, demands it, or unless the specification makes the sequence part of the invention. Amsted's hook was the definite article: claim 1's filters filter "the accelerations," which Amsted said refers back to the accelerations measured by the sensors. But the Board read "the accelerations" as including physical motion of the railcar rather than the signal alone, and the panel agreed. title: 'Time to stop thinking fixed v floating – right now offshore wind needs something in between' - Recharge News
content:
With floating wind commercialising more slowly thank hoped, 'other deepwater' technologies can bridge the gap and keep the industry moving, writes Jonathan Cole For more than two decades, offshore wind has been one of the UK’s greatest industrial success stories. From a nascent technology, offshore wind has evolved into the backbone of a modern, low-carbon energy system, driving investment, creating skilled jobs and positioning the UK as a global leader in renewable energy. That success has never come from standing still or looking backwards. Every major phase of the industry’s growth has required us to challenge accepted wisdom, overcome engineering barriers and push into new frontiers. Larger turbines, deeper waters, longer transmission distances and increasingly complex projects have all become possible because the sector has continually embraced innovation. For several years, the industry has largely viewed this challenge through a binary lens. Conventional fixed-bottom foundations have been seen as the solution for shallower waters, while floating offshore wind has emerged as the long-term answer for the deepest locations. Floating technology will undoubtedly play a major role in the future of offshore wind, unlocking vast new deepwater seabed areas around the world that would otherwise remain inaccessible. However, it cannot be denied that the journey to full commercial maturity has taken longer than many hoped, largely due to challenging economic circumstances and corresponding difficulties in overcoming key industrialisation and infrastructure hurdles. This delay in overcoming such significant barriers should be viewed as part of a complex process, rather than as a failure. Floating offshore wind remains an essential part of our industry’s future. But it does mean we should be willing to ask whether there are additional solutions that can help bridge the gap and accelerate deployment over the coming decade, giving floating more time to fulfil its promise. It is becoming increasingly apparent that such solutions do exist. A new category of “other deepwater” offshore wind is beginning to emerge. These are hybrid foundation concepts designed for intermediate water depths (initially in the 60-90 metre range) that are generally considered too deep for conventional fixed-bottom foundations, but not so deep that floating is the only option. The attraction of these hybrid concepts is that they can combine many of the advantages of fixed-bottom projects with the ability to operate in significantly deeper water. Because many designs build upon proven engineering principles, they can often be simpler to certify and fabricate than fully floating systems. Their slimmer, lighter structures have the potential to reduce manufacturing costs, while making localisation easier by using existing fabrication capability, including tower manufacturers and established steel supply chains. Transportation and installation can be simpler, utilising vessel spreads that are comparable to, or potentially even lesser than, those used for conventional fixed-bottom projects. Additionally, costly new port infrastructure upgrades are unlikely to be required. Once installed, these foundations behave much more like fixed-bottom structures than floating systems. They can support conventional fixed turbines, use static export cables and benefit from operational and maintenance strategies that are already well understood across the industry. In other words, when designed correctly, hybrid structures can offer the possibility of extending many of the efficiencies and supply chain advantages of fixed-bottom wind into deeper waters. This matters because the offshore wind industry needs continuity. Developers require investable projects. Investors need confidence that deployment will continue at a predictable pace. Manufacturers and suppliers need consistent demand to justify expanding capacity and investing in people. If there is a gap between the commercial scaling of conventional fixed-bottom and floating offshore wind, the entire offshore wind ecosystem risks losing momentum. Providing an additional pathway into intermediate water depths could help avoid that outcome. The industry will embrace complementary solutions that accelerate deployment, strengthen supply chains and continue driving down the cost of clean energy. Offshore wind has always advanced because innovators have challenged accepted boundaries and expanded what the industry believed was possible. As we enter the next phase of the sector’s evolution, we should resist thinking in terms of fixed versus floating. title: Horrors of Motherhood | The Haunting of Alejandra by V. Castro - Book Riot
content: Undone women in white are cross-cultural and, as in THE HAUNTING OF ALEJANDRA, there's more to discover beneath the surface of their stories. S. Zainab would like to think she bleeds ink but the very idea makes her feel faint. She writes fantasy and horror, and is currently clutching a manuscript while groping in the dark. Find her on Twitter: @szainabwilliams. Motherhood makes for potent storytelling material. Horror fiction about motherhood highlights the vulnerability and physicality of childbearing and childrearing and all its companion terrors. In The Haunting of Alejandra by V. Castro, motherhood’s many complexities are brought to bear in a story inspired by La Llorona, the haunt of Mexican folklore. After learning the barebones story of La Llorona as a young adult, it inspired both revulsion and a profound curiosity to know more about the mournful murderer of her own offspring. There’s a reason you can find versions of these undone women in white across cultures, from Ireland’s banshee to the hantus of my own background, Malaysia’s langsuir and pontianak. As in The Haunting of Alejandra, they awaken a universal primeval terror, and if you dive deeper you’ll find so much more than what chokes the surface. Note: This book comes with a lot of content warnings, including maternal mortality, attempted suicide, child endangerment, and rape. You’ll find edge-of-your-seat terror and body horror in Castro’s novel, but what makes it satisfying is its clear-eyed and feminist perspective on motherhood. Alejandra’s story is one of generational trauma, colonization, and the endless sacrifices women are expected to make as a reward for bringing life into the world. By taking a critical look at the story of La Llorona and questioning the identity of the story’s real villain, Castro demands that we think twice about maternal pain and grieving. Alejandra is a stay-at-home mom with three children and a husband ever-poised to dismiss her needs. When we meet her, she’s questioning her marriage and life choices, and she’s contending with alienation and isolation. Alejandra loves her children fiercely but increasingly feels defined by them. She can’t identify her value beyond what she provides as a mother and a wife, and it doesn’t help that she has no job, no money, and no family to offer her emotional support. Her relationship with her adoptive parents is strained, and Alejandra was only just getting to know her biological mother when her husband’s work moved them far away from her mom. She’s distanced from her Mexican American culture, but community is the only thing that might help her survive the generational haunting coming for her and her children. When a ghoul appears in her home, Alejandra can only believe she’s spiraling toward a mental break. The veiled creature’s malevolence infects her, telling her she’s worthless and ungrateful, but it isn’t until the monster comes for her children that she determines to look deeper into her family history and seek help from a local curandera to find answers and the strength to fight back. This is speculative body horror you won’t want to miss, especially if you’re looking for stories about motherhood and seeking cultural connections. title: Kim leads ‘V-Day’ events as North Korea highlights Chinese help in Korean War - NK News
content:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended events Monday marking the 73rd anniversary of the “victory in the Fatherland Liberation War” over the U.S., according to state media, emphasizing China’s assistance in the war. The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported Tuesday that the July 27 concert took place at the Pyongyang Indoor Stadium, followed by a small-scale military parade outside the venue to celebrate the so-called victory in the 1950-53 Korean War. The concert included a video segment showing Kim and Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s recent meeting in Pyongyangand clips of Chinese troops during the war. Chinese Ambassador North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended events Monday marking the 73rd anniversary of the “victory in the Fatherland Liberation War” over the U.S., according to state media, emphasizing China’s assistance in the war. The Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported Tuesday that the July 27 concert took place at the Pyongyang Indoor Stadium, followed by a small-scale military parade outside the venue to celebrate the so-called victory in the 1950-53 Korean War. The concert included a video segment showing Kim and Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s recent meeting in Pyongyang and clips of Chinese troops during the war. Chinese Ambassador to the DPRK Wang Yajun and Russian Chargé d’Affaires Vladimir Topekha were invited as special guests. KCNA said attendees were “deeply touched” by the “matchless self-sacrificing spirit, heroism and brilliant feats of excellent sons and daughters of the Chinese people who shared life and death” and fought “shoulder to shoulder” with North Koreans in the war. China entered the Korean War in Oct. 1950, pushing U.S.-led forces back from their advance toward the Chinese border and ultimately stabilizing the front near the 38th parallel. North Korean founding leader Kim Il Sung invaded the South four months earlier in an attempt to unify the peninsula under his rule. Major hostilities were halted on July 27, 1953, with the signing of the Armistice Agreement by the DPRK, China and the U.S.-led U.N. Command. North Korean propaganda continues to call the July 27 holiday the “Day of Victory” while falsely claiming it was a righteous war to repel an invasion by South Korea and the U.S. Monday’s performances were meant as a message of the “DPRK people’s eternal thanks to the brave fighters of the Chinese People’s Volunteers,” KCNA reported, calling the war a joint mission of “resisting America.” “The DPRK-China friendship, based on the shared ideal and militant fraternity, will be immortal along with the history of the great war victory,” it added. Kim also visited the Cemetery of the Fallen Soldiers of the Chinese People’s Volunteers (CPV) on Sunday to pay his respects to Chinese soldiers. He visited the cemetery in October and around the July 27 holiday in 2023 as well, when state media presented a similarly high emphasis on Chinese assistance to mark the 70th anniversary. The focus on China was more subdued at anniversary events in the last two years, but Beijing and Pyongyang have recently appeared to seek closer relations again after the DPRK’s pandemic-era policies slowed down business ties and ended Chinese tourism. State media characterized the celebratory events as an “ideological and mental nutrient” for the North Korean people and military, encouraging patriotism and loyalty to the state. Kim attended the concert with his wife Ri Sol Ju and his young daughter. State TV cameras focused closely on the leader and his daughter during its coverage, as has become standard in recent years, but the KCNA text report did not mention his family’s presence. They didn’t appear at the parade with Kim, who appeared on the viewing platform with current and retired generals, as well as elderly war veterans who should now be in their late 80s and 90s. Kim did not make a speech at this year’s events after doing so at July 27 celebrations in years past. Defense minister No Kwang Chol delivered brief remarks at what KCNA called the “ceremonial parade of the columns symbolic of the units who fought in the Fatherland Liberation War.” He vowed to remain vigilant against “forces that are threatening at every moment,” but did not  include pointed messages at the U.S. and ROK. The parade featured around a dozen block formations, each with 160 young soldiers wearing Korean War-era uniforms and representing divisions named after famous generals and celebrated battles like the “liberation” of Seoul. KCNA praised soldiers who became “human bombs” in the war by carrying out suicide attacks, echoing North Korea’s active policy in the Ukraine war requiring soldiers to kill themselves to complete attacks and avoid capture. Symbolic units of horse-drawn carriages and motorcycles rounded out the historical procession, followed by three formations representing the current-era army, navy and air force to end the parade. Similar concerts and military marches took place at the Pyongyang Indoor Stadium on July 27 in 2024 and 2025 as well, with Kim skipping last year’s events. While North Korea is still engaged in a war alongside Russia against Ukraine, the holiday does not generally serve as a memorial day for all war casualties and Monday’s events appeared mostly focused on the Korean War. Kim also visited the Revolutionary Martyrs Cemetery and the Fatherland Liberation War Martyrs Cemetery in Pyongyang on Sunday. © Korea Risk Group. All rights reserved.

title: Storylines | Royals v. Spirit: A Home Test Against the League Leaders - Real Salt Lake
content: All eyes will be on America First Field this Wednesday, July 29 as Utah Royals FC welcome star forward Trinity Rodman and the Washington Spirit to the Wasatch Front. The midweek matchup will mark the Royals second of three matches played in a congested nine day period. Following the exciting 4-1 victory over the weekend, the home side will look to continue its dominance in front of the home crowd. This edition of storylines will dive into how the Royals have continued to break records in its strongest season in club history, the squad's impressive ability to work as a unit and URFC’s history with the dominant Washington side. Since dropping two matches in its return to NWSL play following the 2026 FIFA World Cup, URFC has bounced-back, winning two consecutive matches to regain the strong form showcased during the first half of the season. While the Royals may not have what is considered as one “big-name” player like opposing squads, the home side has pointed out the importance of every single player on its roster who have worked tirelessly and as one to boost the Royals in its record breaking season towards the top of the NWSL standings. While the Royals have key attacking pieces on its roster like, Canadian forward Cloé Lacasse and Japanese star Mina Tanaka, the squad boasts an impressive nine different goal scorers thus far in 2026, making URFC a difficult team to plan against as any one player from any position can break through to find the back of the net. Utah’s road match against the North Carolina Courage last Saturday, July 25th was the perfect example of this, with four set-piece goals (including penalties) scored by four different players across three different positions. Captain Kate Del Fava opened up the scoring with fellow defender Tatumn Milazzo netting the game winning goal just 18 minutes later, bringing both center backs onto the score sheet in the same match for the first time. While Del Fava earned her first goal in over two years, Milazzo now has a career high three goals in a season. Along with the defenders showcasing brilliance on both ends of the pitch was Tanaka who netted her fifth goal of the season, bringing the Japanese international to an impressive ninth goal contribution of the season (5 goals, 4 assists) to tie Amy Rodriguez (2019) for third in club history. The midfielder continues to bring creativity and high-quality scoring abilities to the pitch, making her a threat to any opposition's defense. The Utah Royals offensive power cannot be explained without the impact of Lacasse, whose stoppage time penalty against the Courage helped to lift the Royals to its 4-1 victory and brought the forward to sole ownership of URFC’s 2026 Golden Boot race with six goals and four assists. The veteran brings a speed and fierce presence to the pitch that not only lifts herself but the whole team in earning results. Lacasse’s 10 goal contributions this season have now brought her equal with the Utah Royals single-season club record set by Christen Press in 2019, with 14 matches left in 2026, the Canadian has ample time to write herself further into Utah’s history books. While the Royals attack has been explosive this season, the work of its backline led by goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn has been key in keeping the squad in matches. With five massive saves on Saturday, McGlynn has continued to showcase her high level ability to read the game and remains a force between the posts with 24 saves and four clean sheets on the season. The veteran keeper will need to continue to work seamlessly with her backline in order to earn a result against the explosive attack of Washington on Wednesday. As the Royals gear up to take on league-leading Washington Spirit on Wednesday night, it is imperative to look back at the squad's history with the visiting side since its return to Utah in 2024. While the Royals overall record of 1-2-2 (W-L-T) against the Spirit looks to favor the visitors, URFC has remained unbeaten in three straight meetings with Washington, taking one victory and two draws. Most recently, the Royals traveled to Audi Field on March 25, 2026 earning a 1-1 draw. While URFC fell behind in the 18th minute, the visitors refused to quit, continuing to pressure on and off the ball in search of a goal. With a belief that never wavered, Tanaka, fresh off an AFC Asian Cup win, netted the equalizer in the 84th minute to help the squad earn a point in what many consider to be one of the most difficult road environments in the NWSL; Washington's home stadium. The Spirit have continued to be a force in the league, with many goal scoring threats on its roster like Italian forward Sofia Cantore who has four goals and one assist on the season. One main attacking threat the Royals will face on Wednesday is USWNT standout, Trinity Rodman. The 24-year-old forward is a force in the offensive third, having used her speed and impressive footwork to net seven goals and five assists thus far in 2026. URFC’s backline will need to work cohesively to thwart any attacks by Rodman in order to keep her off the scoresheet. While the visitors have the attacking power of Rodman, URFC has proven itself as a squad that can exploit opposing defenses and go toe-to-toe with any squad in the NWSL. The key for the Royals in a game where it will undoubtedly see immense pressure, is to get on the scoresheet first. While the home side boasts an impressive 9-2-0 (W-T-L) record when doing so, Washington has yet to lose a match when scoring first earning a 10-0-1 record. Drawing first blood will be an important momentum boost for the home side in its hopes for a victory on Wednesday. The midweek home matchup against the first-place Washington Spirit is scheduled to kickoff at 7 PM MT with tickets still available for purchase. Following Wednesday’s match, URFC remain at America First Field for a second consecutive match, welcoming Sophia Wilson and the Portland Thorns on Sunday, August 2nd. Kickoff is scheduled for 5 PM MT with tickets for both matches are available for purchase here. URFC takes on Washington Spirit at home. title: Trump v. Slaughter: Future Hurdles For DPF-Based EU And UK Data Transfers To The US? - JD Supra
content:
Last month’s Supreme Court decision in Trump v. Slaughter has created uncertainty about the long-standing position of the independence of the Federal Trade Commission. This, in turn, has prompted Max Schrems and his NGO (NOYB) to renew concerns about the Data Privacy Framework (DPF). They have asked the European Commission to review its conclusion that transfers made to participants in the program were adequate under GDPR. It is based on this that the UK adopted its “data bridge” for UK-US transfers. The Court’s decision surrounded Trump’s removal of two FTC commissioners. One of them, Slaughter, challenged this decision; however, in its recent decision the court ruled the President could fire Commissioners "at will" and was not restricted to the historic position relating to their conduct in office. According to the Court, the FTC exercises executive power and therefore falls under the authority of the President, who can thus appoint and remove Commissioners without cause. Schrems argues that as a result of this decision, the FTC is not acting sufficiently independently, and as such cannot be a true independent enforcer of the DPF. And, he argues, it was that independence on which the EU based its adequacy decision. Additionally, he states that reliance on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) may similarly be flawed. Namely, because those rely on transfer impact assessments (TIAs) that assume independent oversight by the FTC. Putting It Into Practice: We do not anticipate that the EU will repeal its adequacy decision on its own. However, this recent statement from Schrems and NOYB suggests that the Framework may be in for a challenge. European or UK companies that transfer data to those in the US, and those who receive such data in the US, should anticipate this. Practical steps to prepare include (1) taking stock of data that is flowing, (2) the basis on which the transfers are being made, and (3) assessing if additional protection measures should be put in place. Updated : July 29, 2026 - 10:14:32 Between stadium performances and global commitments, BTS' V has drawn attention to a book that explores the quiet power of simply getting through everyday life. Late Thursday night, the singer shared on his Instagram story "The Sensibility of an Everyday Person" (a literal translation of the Korean title), a newly published essay collection by the celebrated Korean lyricist Kim Eana. The publisher, Storyseller, said messages poured in almost immediately after V shared the book. "Seeing the response the moment V shared the book reminded us just how much it means to authors and publishers when an artist introduces the books that have inspired them," the publisher wrote on social media. Kim reposted V's story on Instagram with a brief note of thanks addressed to the singer by his given name, Kim Tae-hyung. One of South Korea's most influential lyricists, V has written some of modern K-pop's defining songs, including Park Hyo-shin's poignant ballad "Breath," Brown Eyed Girls' era-defining dance hit "Abracadabra," IU's breakthrough anthem "Good Day" and Ive's self-affirming chart-topper "I Am." If self-help books often promise reinvention, Kim's latest collection argues for something more modest: returning to the rhythms of everyday life. Kim described the book as an exploration of "the small things that saved me when everyday life felt close enough to touch but somehow remained out of reach, when life seemed ever so slightly out of alignment and I felt alone in it." Kim turns her attention to those quietly sustaining an ordinary life. The essays offer comfort to readers who are simply trying to get through each day. "The days that unfold without dramatic highs or lows, without straying from their course, are proof that we're living earnestly," she writes. "How much time and effort does it take to simply keep that going?" Kim writes that finding happiness in such ordinary things is "a tremendous blessing." While everyone naturally strives for a better material life, the quality of that life ultimately depends on whether we have "small moments of happiness we can savor like pieces of candy along the way." The new collection is her first book in six years, following her 2020 bestseller "Ordinary Words," which has sold more than 200,000 copies. V's recommendation arrives as BTS enters another busy stretch. After wrapping up the European leg of its "Arirang" world tour, the group is set to begin performances across North and South America on Aug. 1.                                 IA 51103 Marie Veronica Haley, 92, of Sioux City passed away on Monday, July 27, 2026. A Mass of Christian Burial will be held at 10:30 a.m. Friday, August 7, 2026, at Holy Cross Parish – St. Michael Catholic Church in Sioux City, with Father Randy Schon serving as celebrant. Visitation will be held one hour prior to the service, and a Rosary will be prayed at 9:00 a.m. Interment will be at Calvary Cemetery. Arrangements are under the direction of Meyer Brothers Colonial Chapel. Marie was born in Sioux City on September 20, 1933, to Edward Sr. and Wilma (Hart) Haley. She attended Catholic schools in Sioux City and graduated from Bishop Heelan High School in 1951. She then attended Briar Cliff College, where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1955. While attending college, she was employed by Bishop Heelan High School. Marie later earned a Master of Arts degree from the University of Iowa and completed additional graduate studies at the University of Nebraska, the University of Minnesota, and the University of South Dakota. She began her teaching career in Kingsley, Harlan, and Cherokee before joining the Sioux City Community School District in 1960 as the Library Media Specialist at East High School and later the District Director of Library Services, where she served until her retirement in 1990. She then joined the faculty at Bishop Heelan Catholic High School, retiring in 2002 after 12 years of dedicated service. Marie was a devout Catholic whose faith was the foundation of her life. She also enjoyed cooking, having published several cookbooks, and traveled extensively, visiting Spain, Mexico, England, Ireland, Canada, Alaska, and many other states throughout the country. In recognition of her professional accomplishments, Marie was named one of the Outstanding Young Women of America in 1965. She held numerous leadership positions within the American Library Association, including Chair of the National Supervisors Section and service on its National Board. She also served on the inaugural Board of the Iowa Educational Media Association and was elected its first president in 1972. Marie served as president of the National Alumni Board of Briar Cliff College and was honored as Alumnus of the Year in 1967. She was a member of the original committee that drafted the cable franchise for the City of Sioux City and was a founding member of the Sioux City Library Cooperative, where she served until 2002. In addition, Marie was a past officer and member of the Sioux City School Administrators Association, the NAACP, and the Sioux City Teachers Credit Union. She also served as past president of Mu Chapter of Delta Kappa Gamma, an honorary society for women educators. She was preceded in death by her parents, three brothers: Edward Jr., Wayne, and Paul E. “Gene” Haley, and her sister Pauline (Haley) LaCroix. Survivors include her brother-in-law Emery M. “Mike” LaCroix of Omaha, NE; sister-in-law Marge (Stanek) Haley of North Canton, OH; nieces Diane (Tom) Stock of Columbus, OH, Debbie Russo of North Canton, OH, Terri (Phil) Rossbach of Omaha, NE, Denise Osterhues of Cincinnati, OH, and their families.
